title: Guadalupe
logline: Six in the morning and a question about a war, a white elephant with the wrong answers in it, roses before dawn, a new slice at the Anchor — and the coldest water of the year, on purpose.

previously.text: Theo, from his desk, not turning around: “You were holding it like a rosary.”
At Bastille Julian sang a song called “Magdalena.” Lena watched you hear it, and you looked back.
She took you home. On her bed on Del Playa you said no. She stopped everything, and asked you why.
“I’m not saying the answer’s always going to be no. Not until marriage — I’m not going to tell you that… Just that it’s a big thing for me. And it’s a no right now.” “I can work with that.”
On the porch that leans: “You said no. And you’re still here.” You asked her for daylight. “Sunday. Ellery. I’ll teach you to surf. In *December*.”
At the corner the phone came back on. Lena, 11:41: *Thank you for staying. —L.*

body: The hall comes in with him. For as long as the door is open it lays a slab of fluorescent light across the carpet and both beds, and shows the room whatever there is to see of Jack Costigan at ten past six on the last day of classes: rain beaded on the shoulders of the Carhartt, the Carhartt zipped to the throat, his hair, his mouth, a face that has been up all night and wasn’t trying to sleep. On the far bed a head comes up off the pillow toward the door. Jack gets the door shut behind him with his heel. After that the only light in 412 is on the ceiling.

It comes from Theo’s side, a square of blue-white thrown up onto the tiles by the iPhone lying face up on Theo’s chest. The rest of Theo is a long shape under the duvet, and the square doesn’t waver. Whatever Theo does under it at this hour, it isn’t sleep; Jack has shared a room with him since August and has yet to catch him at it. Over his desk Rosie’s two princes have gone gray in the dark, and the clementine against the lamp has dried hard as a golf ball.

Eighteen minutes from the corner of Del Playa, through the Grove in the first of the rain. His jeans are wet to the shin from the long grass along the Grove path, and his back still has the clothes rack in it. His mouth doesn’t feel like his own yet, and his hands are cold to the wrist from the walk. He sits down on the edge of his own bed in the dark and goes to work on a boot. The laces are soaked and the knot has swelled shut, and he works at it one-handed, because the other hand has the RAZR in it and doesn’t want to put it down. He has been carrying it since the corner. Its outer screen glows up at him from his palm: 6:10. Inside it is the one text from 11:41 last night that he read at the corner and closed and hasn’t answered. The song is in there too, somewhere under the night, and he isn’t going near it.
Over his own bed Nonna’s olive-wood crucifix is a darker shape on the dark wall, about where his head goes. He looks at the boot.
The question comes out of the other bed with nothing in front of it.
“Costigan. Why do you look like you just went through a warzone?”

choices.text: “Couldn’t sleep. Went to look at the ocean.”
choices.key: At ten past six Theo asked why you look like you’ve been through a warzone. You gave him his own line: couldn’t sleep, went to look at the ocean.
response: “Couldn’t sleep,” Jack says. “Went to look at the ocean.”

Theo lies there with it. The square of light holds still on the ceiling. Down the hall the ice machine drops a load into its bin with a noise like a small avalanche, and two floors down a toilet runs and quits, and Theo goes on lying there through both.
“Okay,” Theo says.

He lifts the phone off his chest and holds it up over his face, and it lights him from underneath, chin and cheekbones, somebody about to tell a ghost story. His eyes go once to the RAZR in Jack’s hand, to its little lit screen, and come back up to his own.
The knot gives at last. The boot comes off in Jack’s hand, heavy with the Grove, and he sets it down on the carpet as quietly as a boot can be set down.

response: “Library.”
“Nobody comes back from the library without a book, Costigan.” The square on the ceiling holds perfectly still. “I’ve tried.”
His eyes come down off the ceiling once, to the RAZR in Jack’s hand with its little screen lit, and go back up.
The knot gives at last. The boot comes off in Jack’s hand, heavy with the Grove, and he sets it down on the carpet as quietly as a boot can be set down.

response: “I was out.”
Theo’s eyes go once to the RAZR in Jack’s hand, to the time on its little screen, and come back.
“I know you were out.”
The iPhone turns face down on his chest, and the ceiling goes dark.
In the dark Jack finds the knot by feel and picks at it till it gives, and sets the boot down on the carpet as quietly as a boot can be set down.

body: By twenty-five past six the window has started to come up gray behind the blind, a slat at a time, from the bottom. Jack has the second boot off and has got no further than that. He sits on the edge of the bed in the Carhartt with his socks on the carpet and the boots side by side in front of him, dark to the ankle with wet, like somebody else’s. The rain is still at the glass, small and steady. Out on Ocean Road the first bus of the morning goes by empty and lit up inside, and lays a long bar of light across the ceiling, and takes it away with it.

Delgado is starting up around them: a shower on the far side of the wall, somebody’s alarm going off down the hall and getting hit, and going off again. Somewhere between now and tonight there’s an email to Hale, and the last class of the semester, and sleep, and Jack can’t get any of them to stand still in a line.
Across the room Theo is on his back with the phone dark under his folded hands, looking up at the place where its light was.
“It’s after Thanksgiving,” Theo says.
“I know.”
“I had something in my calendar.”
“It’s been in there since November,” he says after a minute. “It’s very patient.”
In the first gray Theo’s face on the pillow looks younger than nineteen, and very tired. Jack knows which question. He’s the one who put it there.

response: “Ask me.”
“Not at six in the morning,” Theo says. “You’d tell me.” The phone lights under his hands; a thumb taps the glass once; the light goes.

Jack lies back in his clothes with the RAZR shut on his chest and the Carhartt still zipped. The last thing he hears is the rain at the window, and under it, across the room, Theo breathing too evenly to be asleep.
“Move it to Christmas.”
“I’m moving it to Easter.” The phone lights under his hands, and something gets typed into it. “Easter’s very big with you people.”

Jack lies back in his clothes with the RAZR shut on his chest and the Carhartt still zipped. The last thing he hears is the rain at the window, and under it, across the room, Theo breathing too evenly to be asleep.
Jack looks at his boots.
“I’m moving it,” Theo says, and something taps on the screen.

Jack lies back in his clothes with the RAZR shut on his chest and the Carhartt still zipped. The last thing he hears is the rain at the window, and under it, across the room, Theo breathing too evenly to be asleep.

s02.slug: FRIDAY · 11:50 AM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 → THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: Noon gets in around the edges of the blind, white, and lies along the sill. Theo’s bed is empty and made the way Theo makes a bed, with the duvet thrown at the pillow from across the room. The rain has quit. The gutter outside is still working through what’s left of it, a drop at a time onto the ledge, and Jack lies on his back and listens to it and understands, slowly, that he has slept through the last class of the semester and that the semester is not going to come looking for him.
On his desk, where his Dell would be if the Dell had lived past November, Theo’s MacBook sits open with a yellow Post-it stuck across the top of the screen.

body.title: A Post-it
body.text: USE IT. DON’T READ MY MAIL. —T.

body: Behind the Post-it the desktop is a black-and-white still of a boy on a beach, and the mail program is already open, because Theo assumed.
Hale wants it today. Jack sits down in his undershirt and opens a new message and keeps it short, because Hale has opinions about length, and sends it at fourteen minutes past twelve.

body.title: To: Prof. Adrian Hale · Subject: PHIL 9H oral
body.text:
Professor Hale,

I’ll defend Miss Broussard’s argument that a promise is made to a person, not to a reason.

Jack Costigan

body: He sits with it a minute before he sends it.

In 412 the RAZR has one bar on a good day, and this morning it didn’t have that. He takes it out to the east stairwell, and on the landing it finds its bar and remembers everything at once: one new voicemail, 7:12 AM, HOME.
His father left it at twelve past ten, Glenwood Avenue time. Jack puts it to his ear.

“Jack. It’s your father.” A cough, turned away from the phone. Behind him the radio on top of the refrigerator has the morning guys still going about it. “Browns beat Pittsburgh. Last night. Thirteen–six.” That gets a stretch of tape to itself. “Eight sacks.”
There’s a pause then, long enough to hear a spoon go around a cup and one of the radio guys laugh at the other one.
“Thought you’d want to know.”
Paper, close to the mouthpiece. “Your mother left a list by the phone. ‘Ask him about the girl.’” The paper goes down. “I’m not asking you about the girl.”
“Your mother says call.” Then the click, and the woman who lives in the phone asking what he’d like to do with this message.

Jack stands on the landing with the phone still at his ear, grinning at nothing he could point to. It’s twenty past three in Youngstown. His mother is at the school till four, and his father will have gone out to the garage by now, to the space heater and the radio and the Stroh’s fridge, and if Jack called back the phone would ring in an empty kitchen. He can see his father in the recliner last night counting them off on his fingers at the television, all eight, and Nonna telling him to sit down.
He saves it. Out the landing window, open its six inches, the Lagoon lies flat under a low white sky, and an egret stands out in it on one leg with its back to Delgado.
Under the voicemail, at the top of the inbox where he left it at the corner six hours ago, the other one is waiting.

body: He stayed to the end of the song. Then he was out Bastille’s door before ten with his hands in the Carhartt, and when Laney asked where, in front of the table, what he gave her was *Out*.
It’s the last day of classes. Tonight there’s a party at Newman House, ten-dollar limit, carols with the choir, all voices welcome, and everybody he knows will be at it.

journal.title: Dad
journal.text: Frank Costigan. Twenty-six years on the line at Lordstown, laid off since June. Drove me 2,400 miles because two plane tickets cost more than the truck is worth. Saw the Pacific for the first time today. Didn’t say anything. That’s how you know. Monday the 9th: the SUB pay’s done. He went to the bar for the Steelers and didn’t come home. Sat in the employee lot at Lordstown to see if the lights were on. Hit the trash can pulling in at ten to five. Ma called me at one. Nobody was hurt. Saturday he called about Ohio State. Overtime. Pasadena. First time since September. Thanksgiving: sober. Washed the truck. Picked us up at Pittsburgh and talked to Theo the whole way home. Guest says grace — his rule. Told Theo to come back. You don’t call first. Friday morning, a voicemail: Browns beat Pittsburgh. Thirteen–six. Eight sacks. Thought I’d want to know.

s03.slug: FRIDAY · 6:40 PM · A DRUGSTORE IN BUELLTON, OFF THE 101
s03.music: Vince Guaraldi Trio — “Christmas Time Is Here”
body: Somewhere up in the ceiling a choir of children is singing that Christmas time is here, slow, over a piano and a brushed snare, like kids who were promised snow and got told the truth in the car. The drugstore sits off the freeway in Buellton, inland, lit end to end in fluorescent white, and there’s nobody in it but a clerk reading a paperback under the cigarettes and the two of them. The seasonal aisle is a canyon of wrapping paper — candy canes, tartan, a reindeer with a lit nose, a gold foil marked down twice — ending in a cap of the things people buy when they’ve been told to spend ten dollars on somebody they barely know.
Skye has a red plastic basket on her arm, a man’s flannel over a T-shirt from a 10K she didn’t run, and her hair wound up on her head with a Sharpie through the knot, and she is taking meetings.
“You asked to go nowhere,” she said in the lot, when she cut the engine. “This is Buellton. It’s the nearest nowhere I could get on short notice.”

A snow globe first: a church, three houses, a girl skating on a pond the size of a nickel. She shakes it and holds it up and watches the snow come down on the girl until it’s done. “Too sad.” She sets it back exactly where it was. “Snow globes are for people who left.”

A rubber fish on a plaque, which, when she presses the button, turns its head out from the board and sings at them with its mouth half a second behind the words. She lets it finish the verse. “I’ve worked with him,” she says, low, to Jack. “He’s difficult.”

A Chia Pet, the ram. “You said nothing that eats.” “It drinks.” She holds the ram out at arm’s length and gives it back to the shelf. A blanket with sleeves, in a box with a family of four on the front, all of them wearing one on a couch and smiling like hostages. “That family needs help,” she says, and puts it back.

On the bottom shelf, behind a bin of yo-yos, a Magic 8-Ball in a window box. She has it out of the box in the middle of the aisle and shakes it in both hands, and she’s a fortune teller on a pier, all eyelids and vowels, one palm passing slow over the black plastic: “*It is certain.*”
Shake. An agent driving with his knee, the ball pinned under his ear like a car phone: “Babe. Babe. *Cannot predict now.* I’m going into a canyon.”
Shake. A mother on the folding chair by the door of every audition room in Los Angeles, a ballpoint clicking, mouthing the words a half-second ahead: “*Concentrate.* And *ask again.*”

One more, slower, and her face goes kind and sorry: a priest at the church door after the last Mass, holding your hand in both of his because he can see you came in carrying something, wishing for your sake he had better news. “*Reply hazy,*” she says gently, and pats the back of Jack’s hand with the ball. “*Try again.*” Jack has had his hand held exactly like that on the steps of St. Brigid’s since he was tall enough to reach. He laughs.

She tips the ball so the little window catches the light, and the blue triangle swims up out of the dark and settles. “Every answer’s a line reading,” she says. “It’s the only toy in here that admits it.” She turns the box over for the sticker. “Nine ninety-nine. Under budget. You’re a natural.”
“It’s a twenty-sided die floating in blue dye.”
“So is everybody I’ve ever read for.” She shakes it once more and doesn’t look. “Ten yeses, five maybes, five nos. Show me a producer with those numbers.”
In the candy aisle, on the way up front, she wants the room. “Tell me who’s there.”
“Church people. A white elephant. A choir.”
“Good choir?”
“The sign-up sheet says *all voices welcome*. They took it personally.” He picks a roll of Life Savers off the rack for her basket. “And a priest who requests no mistletoe.”
“*Requests.*”
“On the flyer. In capitals.”
“The casserole people,” she says. She drops the Life Savers in with the 8-Ball. “Will they hate me?”
“They won’t meet you.”
“Good.” She adds a second roll, butterscotch, for balance. “I hate being hated on a Friday.”

At the register she lifts the big red bow off the top of a pyramid of boxed candles — the display’s own — and sets it on the counter beside the 8-Ball. The clerk looks at the bow, and at the pyramid without it, and rings it up as a bag of bows. “Separately,” Skye says, and pays for it out of her back pocket while Jack pays for the ball. “The bow’s from me. I want a credit. Small. After the caterer.”

She peels a stick-on tag off a card by the register — TO: and FROM: in red script under a sprig of holly — and presses it onto the box with her thumb. Then she pulls the Sharpie out of her hair, and her hair comes down, and she holds the pen out to him cap first. “You’re the giver,” she says. “Sign it.”

response: He writes it in capitals on the countertop, JACK, and the Sharpie squeaks on the last letter.
She reads it upside down. “Brave,” she says. “What if somebody hates it?”
“It’s a white elephant. Somebody’s supposed to.”
He writes it small, to fit, and runs out of tag on the last S and puts it around the corner.
“Is he in town?”
“He was last Sunday.”
“The one who broke into your dorm?” She takes the box and holds it at arm’s length like a headshot. “I like him. He has range.”
He caps the Sharpie and gives it back to her with the FROM: line empty.
She looks at the empty line, and at him. “Anonymous,” she says. “Very Catholic.”
“Matthew six. Don’t let your left hand know.”
“My left hand knows everything.” She winds her hair back up and stabs the Sharpie through it. “It’s a terrible gossip.”

s03a.slug: FRIDAY · 7:15 PM · THE DRUGSTORE LOT → A SIDE STREET IN BUELLTON
body: Out in the lot the Saab gets one click out of the key and nothing else. She turns it again. Click. The dash lights come up brown and faint and sink back. She tries a third time with her eyes shut, as a courtesy to the car, and gets the click.

He gets the hood up under the lot light. The battery terminals are furred over with a crust, white and green, thick as frost on a Youngstown windshield. He goes at the worst one with the key to the back door on Glenwood Avenue, which still rides on his ring next to the key to 412, and it flakes off in scabs and gets under his nails, and it isn’t enough. Skye goes back into the store. She comes out with a toothbrush already out of its package, held up in front of her like an award.
“I’m a producer now,” she says.
He scrubs. The crust comes away in white dust and black paste. She holds the white iPhone over the engine with its screen turned down for light, and watches him work.
“Where’d you learn this?”
“My dad’s Silverado. Every February, in the driveway, with a kettle.”
“A kettle of what?”
“Hot water. You pour it on the posts.”
She looks back at the drugstore. “I could buy a kettle.”
By the time the posts show dull gray his hands are black to the wrists and there’s a smear across the knee of his jeans where he wiped them without thinking. She tries the key. Click.
She gets out and leans on the fender beside him in the lot light with her arms folded, and looks at his hands, and up at him. “You stood in my rain,” she says. “Now push my car.”
Past the end of the lot a side street runs off between dark houses and tips, just barely, toward the river bottom.

response: She’s in the seat before he’s done saying it, in second with the clutch on the floor, and he walks the Saab out of the lot and onto the side street and gets it rolling, and then running, his black hands on the trunk lid and his boots slapping, the car getting away from him a little more every step under the streetlights — and she lets the clutch out, and the Saab bucks and coughs and catches, and her whoop comes up out of the open top and goes on down the street ahead of her.

She holds it there at the bottom of the street with her foot in it while he walks down to her, wiping his hands on his jeans and making both of them worse. In the front window of the house beside the car there’s a menorah with its first candle burning next to the tall one. She looks at it from the driver’s seat. “Somebody’s starting something,” she says.

She doesn’t let the engine drop below a growl the whole way back — not at the light by the on-ramp, not anywhere. At the Marine Lab turnout, at ten past eight, she pulls up to the chain across the service drive and sits looking at the key. She turns it off, to see. In the quiet the engine ticks as it cools, small and even, a watch somebody left running under the hood. They both look at the key. She turns it. It catches.

When he opens his door the dome light comes on, and she sees his hands in it — black past the knuckles, the crust packed under every nail, one thumbprint on her door handle — and she laughs at them, and at him, and can’t stop. Then she takes his face in both hands and kisses him, long and slow, while he holds his black hands up off her and out of it, a surgeon after the scrub. She lets go. “Go be late to church.”
He switches the RAZR back on halfway up the service road. Down at the chain the Saab honks twice, short.
“It’s an *orphan*, Ohio.” She’s already in the seat, already in second. “There’s no one to call.”

He pushes anyway, out of the lot and down the side street with his black hands on the trunk lid, and on the slope it starts to get away from him, and she lets the clutch out, and it catches on the first try.

“It responds to *physics*,” she says, and puts it in second.

He pushes. It doesn’t catch on the first try, or the second, and on the third, near the bottom of the slope, with him blowing like a horse, it does, and she leans out and bangs the flat of her hand on the outside of her door, twice, which is applause.

s04.music: The St. Brendan’s Choir — “Joy to the World”
body: The carol meets him on the steps before he’s got a hand on the door: an old upright played from the shoulders, a man’s voice on the melody big enough to bring boats in, and twenty more half a bar behind it and gaining. *Joy to the world.* Advent has thirteen days left to run. Inside, they’ve started without it.
Father Osei has the door, in a gray cardigan over the clerical shirt, with a stack of coats over one arm. He looks at Jack’s hands before he looks at Jack.
“You look like a man who has pushed a car.”
“I did.”
“There’s Lava under the kitchen sink.” He stands aside, and the carol goes out past the two of them into the dark, and Jack goes the other way, in.

The front room and the kitchen are one long noise tonight. The plaid couch has been shoved back against the ping-pong table and its dead net; in the corner a Fraser fir carries an angel tipped sideways, listening for something; on the mantel the Advent wreath has its two violet candles going and the rose one waiting. Folding chairs, in rows that held for about a verse. Under the front window the white-elephant table, heaped in paper, with Becca’s clipboard on top. And in the pass-through to the kitchen, in Mrs. Fitch’s cut-glass bowl, the punch — pink, with a crowd around it.

The organist is at the upright in a sweater with a ship’s wheel knitted into the front, bringing his hands down on the chords like he means to be heard in Monterey. Mrs. Fitch is at his shoulder with a cup of punch and the descant. “Gus,” she says, between lines, “you’re *dragging*.” He doesn’t speed up. Gus. A semester of Sundays, and the voice has a name.

The Lava is where the priest said, behind the Comet, a gray bar worn down to the shape of somebody’s grip. Jack runs the tap as hot as it goes and does one hand at a time. The left waits its turn over the front pocket of his jeans, over the RAZR, black to the wrist, leaving a print on the denim. Behind him, at the pass-through, Laney’s drawl at the punch bowl stops in the middle of a word and doesn’t start again for a while. The porch door opens on Julian’s laugh, and on a voice under it that Jack would know in a stadium. He keeps his eyes on the water.

body.text: On the other side of the counter the ladle goes into the bowl and comes out, and a cup gets filled, and whoever filled it stays there, long enough that he can feel her at the edge of things. He works the Lava into his knuckles and doesn’t turn. Then, to the punch: “*Delaney*,” and her steps go back out to the front room.

From the other side of the counter, over the ladle: “Jack.” He lifts one wet hand off the soap without turning around, and goes on scrubbing. Behind him the ladle stops, and starts again. Then, to the punch, with feeling: “*Delaney*.” And Julian, warmly, from somewhere at her elbow: “Evening, Jack.”

body: Jack turns the tap back on and goes to work on the other hand. He scrubs till the water runs gray and stays gray. The black comes off the backs of his hands; under the nails it stays, and will, he can tell, for days. When he looks up again the pass-through is full of other people.

Becca comes around into the kitchen with the clipboard on her hip and finds him at the sink. “Line three! You *came*.” She shows him: COSTIGAN, in her block capitals. “Ten dollars, nothing that eats. Mrs. Fitch is checking.”

Tyler Brandt comes in for punch and stays for the sink, a hand like a catcher’s mitt on Jack’s shoulder. “Brother. Brian Kelly.” He looks down into the Lava. “He left an *undefeated* team. In the *night*. For Notre *Dame*. I’m from Cincinnati. I don’t know whether to pray for him or *at* him.”

Bridget is at the coffee urn by the back door, filling it from a can of Folgers, and she’s the only one tonight who looks at his face instead of his hands. She puts a dish towel over his shoulder on her way past and doesn’t say anything about it.

In the front room Joey Abruzzo is explaining to two sophomores from the choir, at volume, that four of Mrs. Fitch’s lemon bars count as one if they’re touching. Peter Haddad is up a stepladder straightening the angel with Kenzie holding the ladder for him; he gets the angel upright and lets go, and the angel leans again.
Theo comes in off the porch in a black cashmere turtleneck and takes up a place against the refrigerator beside Laney, who is in black velvet to the knee. “You match,” Jack says, scrubbing.
“We’re in mourning,” Laney says.
“For what?”
“Advent,” says Theo.

Margot has the step stool in the corner by the back door and a Moleskine open on her knee. “For the column,” she says, when he looks at the notebook. “Field notes on a Catholic Christmas party, held, I’m informed, in Advent.”
Then, without looking up from the page: “Six-ten this morning.” Her window, 305, is over the front walk. “I’ve stopped counting. It was getting sad.”
Kevin is by the refrigerator in a green sweater with a white snowflake across the chest that his mother mailed from San Jose, worn, he has told everybody, out of love and under protest.
“The bell works,” he tells Jack, low. “Doug got as far as the hall Wednesday. I walked him back.” He tastes the punch, and looks at Laney.

The punch is peppermint schnapps and something clear that Laney, asked, calls “a Texas thing,” and it has been working on Mrs. Fitch for three cups. On the second verse she comes in a third above everybody, high and sure and gloriously in tune, and Gus turns half around on the bench to see where it’s coming from. Father Osei comes through with the coats put away, takes a cup, tastes it, and holds it up to the light over the stove. Laney is studying the angel. Osei sets the cup down, lifts the whole bowl off the pass-through in both arms, and puts it on top of the refrigerator next to the fire extinguisher. “Gaudete is Sunday, Miss Price,” he says. “You’re early.”
Kevin reaches into the black velvet clutch under Laney’s arm and comes out with a silver flask the size of a prayer book. “Respectfully,” he says, and it goes into his own back pocket.

By the tree Theo has his iPhone out, and he reads off it, for everybody, in his voice for the intentions at the twelve-ten, grave and even, as if he were asking prayers for the sick: “…*an indefinite break from professional golf.*”
Mrs. Fitch, between verses, to her hymnal: “Good. He should go home.”

Laney was in the front room getting out of her coat when the priest said it at the door. She leans on the pass-through on both elbows and looks down at his hands in the sink. “Fireman. Whose car did you *push*?”

response: “Kevin’s.”
Kevin, from the refrigerator, turning Laney’s flask over in his hand: “My mother’s car is a Honda. Hondas start.”
By the tree Theo has put his phone away and is watching Jack’s hands.
“The Pope’s.”
“The Pope has a *driver*.” She takes a sip of what’s left in her cup, sorrowfully, since it’s the last of it.
By the tree Theo has put his phone away and is watching Jack’s hands.
“A friend’s.”
Laney looks at him over the rim of her cup for longer than she looks at anybody, and drinks.
By the tree Theo has put his phone away and is watching Jack’s hands.

s05.slug: FRIDAY · 9:05 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE WHITE ELEPHANT
body: At five past nine the folding chairs come back into rows, and Becca stands in front of the white-elephant table with the clipboard in one hand and Mrs. Fitch’s Advent-candle box in the other — the long white one the tapers came in, full now of folded slips — and waits for quiet until she has it.

Jack takes the last folding chair in the back row, by the kitchen door. The room is in front of him and the tree is at the far end of it, and Lena is up there by the tree on a folding chair next to Julian’s. He keeps it that way.

“Okay! My uncle calls the cattle auction at the Kootenai County Fair, and I’ve been listening to him since I was four, so we’re doing this right. You draw a number. When it’s your number you open something or you steal something. Three steals and it’s frozen. No crying, Joey.”

She unfolds the first slip and goes into her uncle’s chant with no warning at all, level and fast, the numbers running together into something you could almost sing — *one-one-who’s-got-a-one-I-got-a-one-one-one* — and Bridget, who has the one, goes up to the table laughing with both hands over her face.

It goes fast. Theo’s gift is an unopened can of spray tan, still in its cellophane; Father Osei draws four and opens it in front of everybody and reads the label all the way down to *streak-free*. “I shall treasure it,” he says. “In a drawer.” Julian’s is a mix CD in a sleeve he lettered by hand, and it goes to Kevin, and Julian lifts a hand from beside the tree: “Nothing of mine. I’m not that guy.” Laney’s is a foam koozie with SUGAR across it in rhinestones; it goes to Tyler, who fits it onto his punch cup at once and wears it the rest of the night. Peter Haddad draws a flat box that turns out to be Bridget’s, a Theology of the Body workbook for teens with a sunset on the cover, and holds it up for the room, and Kenzie goes very still beside him, and Peter says, “Great. *Great*,” and puts it under his chair. “Chastity,” Margot says from the step stool, writing it down. “Now with sunsets.” Between numbers Becca tells the room that Thomas flies to Idaho next week, in his Tupperware, under the seat in front of her, because it’s on her mind.

Jack’s number comes up early. He goes to the table and takes the heaviest thing on it, a brick done up in brown grocery-bag paper and kitchen string, and the room has watched him pick it before he’s got the string off: a can of Café du Monde, orange and yellow, and a pound of Community Coffee in the red bag. The tag is a strip of index card, punched and tied on, in a hand he knows.
*FOR WHOEVER. BREW IT STRONG. —L.*

journal.title: Becca Lindell
journal.text: Coeur d’Alene. Seven siblings; wants seven or nine kids, odd numbers, for the tiebreaker. Can butcher a deer — elk too. Has pulled a calf, and it shows. Ran the beach cleanup like a cattle drive and put me on her team. Asked about the scar in the water. Told her mother the cleanup was a date, then asked me if it was. Wrote FRIDAY? on her clipboard, and meant it. Drives her brother Eli’s red Ranger; St. Isidore on the visor. Second date: Friday-night football. Knows downs. Prayed a Glory Be on fourth and one. Learned the First Way on the bleachers and said it back perfectly. Kissed my cheek so there’s no confusion. Third date was mine. I asked. I paid. The elephant seals at Piedras Blancas at sunset, in Kevin’s Odyssey. She knew what every one of them weighed. Nobody’s ever planned a thing for her, she says. She’s been praying for two in the morning. Named a hermit crab Thomas, after the First Way, and asked Fr. Osei whose blessing it was. Works the Marine Lab touch tank Thursday afternoons and Friday at six in the morning — that’s how she signed Thomas out. He’s home; she knows him by the chip in his shell. Mailed Rosie a birthday card with Thomas on it and six true facts on the back, to the address I gave her for her Christmas cards. She does them in October. Has a page on her clipboard for Wes. She’s been praying for him and Lena since September. Her eyes are gray. Brought a survival bag to the library for my midterm, with a clementine for Lena. Prays at two, like always. Took me to *Where the Wild Things Are* at the Rialto; her favorite line is the last one. My mother wrote her a thank-you note. Her list for Halloween says WE SHOULD MATCH!! It’s due Halloween. She says I look at her like homework. She says she’ll wait. Stuck on the touch tank all weekend while we were at Big Sur: the weekend volunteer has the swine flu. Asked me for the monks’ fruitcake for her Grandma Agnes — the only honest fruitcake in America. I handed in my homework six days early. St. Isidore and St. Maria: her first. Early, she said. Nobody’s early but her. Halloween: she sewed my costume out of a Rathdrum Feed & Seed sack. She was St. Maria de la Cabeza in Mrs. Fitch’s lace, with a water jug. Best Saint, by acclamation — a gold halo. Never won anything that wasn’t a heifer. Home at 11:40 for the six o’clock tank; the volunteer still has the flu. ‘Farmer.’ Theo’s birthday: huckleberry jam from her mother, for Theo — the Idaho gift. Next to his mother all night. ‘He’s *mine*. Since the beach cleanup.’ Toasted St. Martin de Porres: a dog and a cat and a mouse, one bowl. The Portolá steps, November 4th: her mom’s been calling me her boyfriend since September. She asked if she could tell her she’s right. I said yes. Her mom first, then Facebook. She flies home to Spokane the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. Her mother has named the turkey. She asked how I’m getting home. Greyhound. She frowned. Her mother sent a box: socks, cookies, two jars of huckleberry — JACK, and FOR THE CATHOLIC ROOMMATE. She offered me Daisy’s money. Six hundred and twelve dollars. It’s there, she says. Daisy doesn’t mind. Saturday, Ohio State in overtime: she gave me a photograph of the elephant seals in a frame she painted, every seal labeled with what it weighs. She’ll call during her dad’s grace on Thanksgiving so I can hear it. She wants to watch Michigan here, with me. ‘Someday I want to see your house. Is that okay to say?’ Ma wrote her. Three days after Christmas. Pittsburgh’s cheaper than Cleveland. She looked. Wednesday, in Eli’s truck, I told her. She said she did everything right, and she did. ‘It just isn’t the thing, is it.’ She asked me to leave it up on Facebook till she’s told her mom at the table. Thursday at two she texted. Still praying for me — not a girlfriend thing, she says. At the twelve-ten she turned around across the aisle at the sign of peace and held out her hand. Then she held it out to Lena. At the airport, a week to the day: St. Raphael, for Nonna. Father Osei read the name at the twelve-ten, and she heard. Thanksgiving: told her mom at the table. Texted me first — happy Thanksgiving, praying for Nonna, taking it down now. Then she did. The Immaculate Conception, on the steps after the 12:10: white elephant, ten dollars, nothing that eats. Thomas is going home to Idaho in a Tupperware to see snow. The Advent party: ran the white elephant like a cattle auction. Three steals and it’s frozen.

response: He stands at the table with the coffee in the crook of one arm and the strip of index card between his finger and thumb, and keeps his eyes on it — the capitals, the dash, the L — because the tree is where his eyes would go next, and he knows it. Then Becca is chanting the next number, and he goes back to the last chair in the back row with it on his knees, and after a while he puts it under his chair.

response: “Who brings coffee to a white elephant?” he says to Tyler, in the next chair.
Lena answers from her folding chair by the tree, loud enough for everybody. “A woman from New Orleans. We bring coffee to *funerals*.”
Somebody laughs. Jack laughs with Tyler, at the floor between his boots, and doesn’t look up the room, and Becca’s already chanting the next number.
He puts it under his folding chair, tag side down, and sits on the chair over it.

s05a.slug: FRIDAY · 9:20 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE WHITE ELEPHANT
body: Joey Abruzzo has number nine and goes for the 8-Ball like it called his name: a white plastic bag with a big red bow stuck on the outside. He gets the box out and holds it over his head in both hands, and Becca reads the tag off the side of it for the room.

body.text: “*From Jack!*”
“*From St. Nicholas!*” — and up by the tree a folding chair creaks, once, as somebody in it sits up.
“From… nobody, it’s blank, that’s okay!”

body: Joey gets the ball out of the box and shuts his eyes and holds it against his chest. “Will I,” he says, to the whole of Newman House, “be a *priest*?” He shakes it once, hard, and turns it over, and opens his eyes, and reads it in the little window.
*It is decidedly so.*

Newman House loses its mind. Joey is on his feet with the ball over his head — “IT’S *DECIDED*” — and Tyler comes across two rows of folding chairs to bump his fist, and Gus plays a chord on the upright that might be a fanfare. At the back Father Osei raises his cup to the boy.
Three numbers later it’s Lena’s. He hears her chair scrape back by the tree, and her heels cross the front of the room, and stop at Joey’s row. “I need it for Hale’s oral.”
“That’s my *vocation*.”

“That’s one steal!” Becca makes a mark. There’s a scuffle of folding chair, and Joey, politely: “Excuse me.” “Two!” Then Lena, without any hurry at all: “Thank you, Joseph.” “*Three!*” Becca’s pen comes down on the clipboard. “Frozen! She keeps it!” Joey sits back down and looks at his empty hands, and then at Tyler, entirely at peace. “It’s fine,” he says. “It already told me.”

Jack keeps his eyes on the back of Tyler’s folding chair. The room goes on without her for a minute — somebody laughing, Becca asking what it said and getting nothing for it — and when he lets the front of the room back into the edge of his eye, she’s in her chair beside Julian again with a hand over the pocket of her cardigan.

body.text: When the next number has been called and the noise has moved on, she says it across the room, over everybody’s heads. “Thank you, Jack.” He nods at the back of Tyler’s folding chair, as if Tyler had said it, and Becca calls sixteen.
Across the room he can feel her look for him, once, over everybody’s heads. He keeps his eyes on Becca’s clipboard and leaves it with the saint.

body: Mrs. Fitch draws thirteen and opens a glow-in-the-dark rosary, which is Kenzie’s, and says it’s lovely and she has nine. Margot draws fourteen and steals it off her — “For the column” — and holds it up under the lamp to charge it, and sits back down with it glowing faintly green in her lap while she writes. “That’s a steal!” Becca says, and makes her mark, so happy about the rules working that Mrs. Fitch can’t mind.
Becca unfolds the next slip and the chant starts up again, *fifteen-fifteen-who’s-got-fifteen*, and under Jack’s chair the coffee is where his heel can find it.

s06.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE UPRIGHT
body: At twenty to ten Gus gets the choir back up, and it is all voices welcome, and they’ve come. Gus on the melody, wide and flat and immovable. Mrs. Fitch’s descant, a third over the top, three cups to the good. Joey half a step under everybody and proud of it. Kenzie Rourke with the one gorgeous voice in the room, so that every time she comes in the carol gets better around her. And under all of it, from back by the refrigerator, a real bass — low and warm and dead on the note — and it’s Kevin.
“Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose,” Kevin says, when the verse is over and Jack is staring at him. “My mother made me.”

Jack has been in the kitchen since the last number was called. The Lava came off his hands an hour ago and he’s found reasons since — the cups, the trash, Mrs. Fitch’s lemon-bar pans soaking in the sink — and from the kitchen door the front room is a long gold box with the upright at the far end of it, and Lena at the far end of the upright, and the width of a whole party in the way. That’s where he has kept it all night.

Father Osei’s rule is on an index card taped to the music stand since Thanksgiving — ADVENT HYMNS UNTIL DEC. 24. THANK YOU. G.O. — and Mrs. Fitch has just started “Joy to the World” again from the top, by herself, and Gus has gone after her, because he always does.
Jack, in the kitchen door with a dish towel over his shoulder, says it to Becca, but it carries. “It’s Advent. You don’t cut the cake at the engagement party.”
Becca thinks about it. “At my cousin’s engagement party they *did* cut the cake,” she says. “It was a sheet cake. It said CONGRATS.”

From the far end of the upright, over the hymnals, Lena answers. “On the river they start the levee bonfires the week after Thanksgiving. Logs and cane, a whole cabin out of wood, every half mile up the levee in St. James Parish, all of it for one night. Nobody down there says it’s cheating on Christmas Eve. The building *is* Advent.” Then, louder, to the kitchen door: “And ‘Joy to the World’ isn’t a Christmas carol. Isaac Watts wrote it about the Second Coming. It’s Psalm Ninety-Eight. It’s the most Advent song in the hymnal.”

journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him.

choices.text: “‘The Lord *is* come.’ Past tense. Watts was hedging.”
response: “‘The Lord *is* come,’” Jack tells Becca. “Past tense. Watts was hedging.”
It carries. From the far end of the upright: “Watts was a *Congregationalist*, Jack. He hedged for a living.”
Becca looks from him to the upright and back. “She got you,” she says, pleased with everybody.
Father Osei passes the upright with a tray of lemon bars, at no particular speed. “Miss Broussard is correct, it is still Advent, and Mrs. Fitch is seventy-one. Sing.”

Gus brings his hands down. Jack sings it into the sink with the towel on his shoulder — *Joy to the world, the Lord is come* — and somewhere out past the kitchen wall an alto comes in a good deal louder than the song needs, and he keeps his own voice down at the soap, under Kevin’s, with Mrs. Fitch sailing over the top of everybody. He never goes to the door.

response: He doesn’t answer. He goes back to the sink and runs the water. Out front there’s a space after her last word about the size of the answer he usually gives her, and nobody fills it, and then Mrs. Fitch comes back in on the descant.

Gus brings his hands down. Jack sings it into the sink with the towel on his shoulder — *Joy to the world, the Lord is come* — to the soap and the window over the sink, under Kevin’s bass, with Mrs. Fitch sailing over the top of everybody. Somewhere out past the kitchen wall there’s an alto in it, and he doesn’t go looking for it.
“Then Mrs. Fitch is a prophet,” he tells Becca.

It carries. Becca laughs out loud, the cattle-auction laugh, and at the far end of the room somebody else laughs before she means to; he hears it from the kitchen door, and hears it stop, and doesn’t turn to see what she does with her face.
Father Osei passes the upright with a tray of lemon bars, at no particular speed. “Miss Broussard is correct, it is still Advent, and Mrs. Fitch is seventy-one. Sing.”

Gus brings his hands down. Jack sings it into the sink with the towel on his shoulder — *Joy to the world, the Lord is come* — and Becca sings it beside him, loudly and exactly in tune, with Mrs. Fitch sailing over the top of everybody. He never goes to the door.

s06a.slug: FRIDAY · 10:00 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE UPRIGHT
body: Gus plays the last chord, and holds it, and lets it go, and gets up off the bench working his fingers. They’re a fisherman’s hands, thick through every knuckle, with a white seam across the back of the left, the kind a line leaves when it runs through a hand. He looks around for his punch. His punch is on top of the refrigerator. “Somebody spell me,” he says. “Does anybody play?” The room looks at its shoes.
Joey’s hand goes up. “I can do ‘Heart and Soul.’”
“Joey,” says Becca, “it’s *Advent*.”
Kenzie looks at Peter, and Peter looks at the tree. Gus waits with his fingers laced, cracking them one at a time.
Mrs. Fitch says she would, but she’s had three, and she knows it, and the Lord knows it.
Margot, from the step stool, still writing: “I took piano. I won’t be taking questions.”
Nobody on the plaid couch moves. Jack knows who’s on the arm of it without looking: she went there when the singing stopped.

Jack has heard her play. The basement upright in Delgado, properly, around its dead F, at one in the morning with the dryers going — her left hand stepping over the hole in the keyboard every time it came, the way you’d step over a board you knew was loose — and he has heard her say why she doesn’t where people can hear. If you play well, people ask you to play.
He doesn’t look over. He knows the shape of her sitting very still on the arm of a couch, and he leaves it at the edge of things, where he has kept it all night.

response: He keeps his mouth shut and his eyes on Gus. At the edge of things something on the arm of the couch turns toward him, and he lets it, and keeps looking at Gus.
Then Julian, by the tree, says he can play a little.

response: “Julian plays,” Jack says.
Julian, surprised and then pleased, puts his cup down on the mantel and goes to the bench. Jack finds something to do with the dish towel while Julian crosses the room, and keeps finding it.

response: “I’ll turn pages,” Jack says.
“There are no pages, son,” says Gus. “It’s Advent. We go by ear.”
And Julian, who has come up from the tree to stand beside him, sits down on the bench.

s06b.slug: FRIDAY · 10:25 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE KITCHEN SINK
body: The punch cups are Mrs. Fitch’s, cut glass to match the bowl, forty of them, and they don’t go in any machine. Father Osei has them in the sink in water as hot as the tap will give, his sleeves rolled to the elbow, the wooden rosary on his belt knocking the cabinet door every time he reaches for the bottom. The mistletoe lies on the drainboard beside the Lava where he set it down, tape and all. The dish towel has been over Jack’s shoulder since half past eight. Osei hands a wet cup back to him over his shoulder, and the towel has a job.

Through the doorway Julian has gone from the carols into something slower that Jack doesn’t know, and Lena’s alto is under it, keeping it company. Jack stands with his back to the doorway and dries. When the alto drops out for a bar, his hands stop on the cup until it comes back.
Osei talks, and none of it is about Jack. It’s about waiting rooms.

“At the hospital in Kumasi the waiting room was the honest room in the building,” he says, rinsing. “Wooden benches. A fan in the ceiling that went round when there was power. Mothers with babies, old men with their sons, a farmer who had walked since morning with his hand wrapped in a shirt. Once a goat, which belonged to somebody and was also unwell.” Another cup comes back over his shoulder. “Everyone in it was exactly where they were. Upstairs on the wards everybody pretended — the patients that they felt better, the doctors that they knew. Downstairs people only waited, and told each other what for.”
He holds a cup up to the light over the stove, finds a print on it, and puts it back in the water.
“Advent is a waiting room with candles.”

He takes one of Jack’s hands off the towel and turns it over, and looks at the black still under the nails. “Battery acid,” he says. “Lava will not reach it. Lemon. Mrs. Fitch keeps a bag of lemons in the bottom of the refrigerator for the lemon bars.” He considers the refrigerator, and the punch bowl on top of it. “Do not tell her who told you.”

Over the stove hangs a clock shaped like a teapot that somebody gave Newman House in a better decade. Twenty-five past ten. Jack looks at it, and when he looks away from it Osei’s eyes are just leaving it too, and going back to the cups.

response: “I’ve got somewhere to be.”
Osei rinses a cup and turns it in the light. “In Kumasi, a guest who leaves before the singing is finished is either in love or in debt.”
“Which am I?”
“I was a doctor.” He hands the cup across. “I don’t diagnose at parties.”

He pulls the plug, and the sink starts down with a long complaint in the pipes. “Saturday I am in the closet at half past three,” he says, drying his own hands on his trousers, since Jack has the towel. “And my door is the one with the light on. I sleep badly. It may as well be useful.”
He holds out his hand for the towel. Jack gives it to him, and Osei folds it once over the oven handle and squares it there. “Ɛyɛ,” he says, and goes back out to his party.

Osei moves the sprig on the drainboard away from the clean cups with the back of a wet wrist. “With the spray tan, a flask from 2007, and a collar that belonged to a ferret.” He goes back to the water. “It is a very ecumenical drawer.”

“I do,” Osei says, surprised to be asked. “It is cheaper than worrying, and it works on Tuesdays.” He hands back the last cup. “And on Fridays, if you are not fussy.”

s06c.slug: FRIDAY · 10:45 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE STEPS → OCEAN ROAD
body: By a quarter to eleven Newman House is coming apart the ordinary way. Becca and Mrs. Fitch are carrying folding chairs back into the hall closet by twos and counting them against each other. Gus is playing something with no words to the emptying room. At the bottom of the steps a pair of headlights swings across the olive tree: Julian, bringing the car around. Laney is asleep upright on the porch swing in her black velvet, with the clutch in her lap and her mouth a little open.

Theo went at half past ten, back toward Delgado, with a lemon bar in a napkin and the turtleneck up to his ears. Kevin carries Laney’s coat down to the curb and stands there with it over his arm, waiting for Julian’s car.
“She made it, she drank it,” Lena says. “She’s a closed system.”
At the sink, at half past ten, the RAZR went once against his hip.

body: Becca comes out with a folding chair under each arm and stops beside Jack on her way to the closet. “You got the coffee!” she says. “That was the best one. I *wanted* that one.” She goes on with the chairs.

Margot comes out past him buttoning her coat and stops beside Jack on the top step. Under the porch light she writes one more line in the Moleskine, and then, this once, turns it around and holds it out to him.
*The punch was the only thing in the room that wasn’t waiting.*
She doesn’t underline it. She shuts the book and goes down the steps with her hands in her pockets.

Behind him Lena has got Laney off the swing and down onto the top step; he can hear Laney go back to sleep inside a minute, small and even, against somebody’s shoulder. Julian’s headlights come up the drive and stop, and Julian comes up the steps for Laney’s shoes, which are under the swing, and carries them back down by the straps. On the way past he touches Jack’s arm. “Good night, Jack. Merry Christmas, if I don’t see you before.”
“Ride with us?” Lena says. “There’s room if Laney lies down.”

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven.

s06m.slug: FRIDAY · 10:10 PM · NEWMAN HOUSE, THE KITCHEN DOOR
body: Julian plays by ear. He takes Gus’s tempo for a verse and then, kindly, a better one; he finds a key Kevin can sit at the bottom of and leaves the floor of it open for him; he gives Father Osei “O Come, O Come, Emmanuel” in a minor so plain it sounds older than the house, and then, without stopping, lifts it into “Joy to the World” for Mrs. Fitch, who puts down her cup; when her descant goes up, his left hand goes down an octave to hold the floor under her. He doesn’t look at his hands. Somewhere in it there’s an alto at his shoulder, and where Julian’s voice won’t go, hers goes.
Jack watches Julian’s hands from the kitchen door, leaning on the jamb, with the dish towel. Julian’s hands, and the keys, and nothing to the left of them.

“Costigan. Move.” Theo has a kitchen chair. Jack moves a step back into the kitchen, and Theo climbs up on the chair in his loafers and tapes a sprig of something green with white berries to the top of the doorframe, tearing the Scotch tape with his teeth. “Picture it,” he says. “A doorway. Two Catholics. A plant with a record.” The plant is contraband: FR. OSEI REQUESTS NO MISTLETOE is on the flyer on the corkboard, three feet away, in capitals. Out in the front room Laney, awake for the purpose, has a hand on Lena’s elbow the minute the carol ends — “Magdalena, come help me with the cups, I am *so* drunk” — and Theo gets down off the chair and takes Jack by the sleeve.
Kevin comes through with a stack of paper plates and says it low, to both of them. “Leave it alone.”
Theo doesn’t let go of the sleeve. Laney doesn’t let go of the elbow.

It doesn’t matter. Julian is up from the bench with a paper cup of water from the bathroom tap, because Lena has sung herself dry, and he gets to the kitchen door when she does, and stops there because she has, and looks up, because Theo’s tape is shining in the light. He smiles. He kisses her cheek, gently, with his free hand under the cup so it won’t spill.

Jack sees it from four feet away. He has kept his eyes off her all night — the length of the room, the kitchen wall, the backs of people’s heads — and he has nothing left to keep them off her with now. He looks. It’s the only time all night he lets himself. She’s coming up from under it with the cup in her hand, and her eyes go past Julian’s shoulder straight to him, as if they knew where he’d be, and find his face before he’s done anything to it. Her own face changes, all at once, into something he hasn’t got a word for, and she doesn’t look away. Her lips part, the way they do before she says his name, and don’t get there. He’s the one who turns back to the sink.
Theo, in retreat, climbs back on the chair to get the evidence down, and comes off it into the doorway at the same moment as Tyler Brandt with a tray of empty cups. They both look up.
“Brother,” says Tyler.
“*Absolutely* not,” says Theo.

Father Osei crosses the front room, limping a little, reaches up past both of them, and takes the mistletoe down, tape and all. “I requested,” he says, and carries it into the kitchen at arm’s length.

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek.

s07.slug: FRIDAY · 11:20 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: Since Thursday the strand around her window has lost more ground. What still burns has pulled back into the bottom right corner of the frame, a knot of red and green and one white gone stubborn yellow, so the light in her room comes up off the sill from one side, low, like footlights somebody quit hanging halfway through.

They came in by the alley. The rack is where it was, and the jar of beach glass with the blue piece on top, and the O’Connor on the sill with CON struck through. The floor has been picked up since Thursday; his shirt isn’t on it. The white dress still hangs on the back of the door in the cleaner’s bag, its collar standing up under the paper. Skye lifts it off the hook by the hanger and hangs it on the rack between two flannels, and pats the bag once.
“She’s had a big week,” she says.
“Second time anybody’s been up here,” she says over her shoulder. “You’re a regular. It’s alarming.”
She takes his right hand and turns it over under the lights. The Lava got the backs of it. The black is still packed under the nails, a thin crescent of her battery under every one.
“You washed.”
“There was soap.”
“Most of my car’s still on you,” Skye says, and keeps the hand.

She wants the party, all of it, from the door. He gives it to her sitting on the end of the mattress with his boots off and her feet in his lap: the priest at the door in a cardigan, who took one look and knew he’d pushed a car; the organist at the upright with a voice like a foghorn, a measure behind on every verse and not sorry; a parish secretary, seventy-one, three cups into a punch somebody from Texas had done something to, sailing the descant a third above everybody; the priest tasting the punch and putting the bowl on top of the refrigerator. His roommate’s spray tan, unopened, going home with the priest. He leaves out the upright, and the kitchen doorway, and what was hanging in it. She watches his face go past that part, and lets it go by.
“Do her,” Skye says. “The secretary.”
“You’ve never heard her.”

“Do I need to?” She stands up on the mattress in her socks with one hand on the window frame and her chin in the air, and sings *Joy to the world* a third above anywhere it has ever lived, with a quaver in it like a kettle coming up and the total confidence of three cups, and holds the last note until the frame creaks under her hand. It’s terrible. It’s not far off.

He tells her the white elephant: a girl with a clipboard running it like an auction, steals allowed, three steals and it’s frozen. A kid named Joey got her bag, bow and all, and shook the 8-Ball with his eyes shut and asked it if he was going to be a priest, and it said *It is decidedly so*, and the room went up like somebody had scored. And then there were steals.

response: “A friend,” he says.
“In italics?”
He says nothing. She looks at him over her knees with her head on one side, long enough that he knows she heard it, and lets it be.

“It went to a good home.”

“Smart,” Skye says. “Never tell anybody your question. They give you notes on it.”

s07a.slug: FRIDAY · 11:45 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: By a quarter to twelve his flannel and her sweater are on the floor with the scripts, and she’s lying on top of him in a black bra and her jeans with her chin on her stacked hands in the middle of his chest, looking at him down her nose, what’s left of the lights in the side of her hair.
“I’ve been doing coverage on your sentence,” she says.
“Coverage.”

“It’s what readers do. You read the script and write two pages on why it doesn’t work.” She takes one hand out from under her chin and holds up a finger. “One. It isn’t a rule. You said so yourself — not always, not till marriage, you don’t know that about you. A rule I’d respect. I’ve worked union.” A second finger. “So it’s a schedule. And a person’s allowed to ask what’s on a schedule. That’s what a schedule is *for*.”
“It’s not a schedule. It’s a no.”
“It’s a no with a date on it.”
“I didn’t put a date on it.”

“You put *now* on it. Now is a very specific date.” She taps his breastbone on *now*. “Your Church has a candle for rejoicing and a Sunday it’s due. You told me so. Don’t lie there and tell me Catholics don’t keep a calendar.”

She rolls off him long enough to unbutton her jeans and work them down her legs and kick them off the end of the mattress, and rolls back on, and doesn’t lose her place. “Costume change. Two. It had a time on it. A quarter past four, Friday morning. That was nineteen and a half hours ago. I’ve done live television, Jack. *Now* lasts about four seconds. After that it’s a rerun.”

A third finger. “And in my business you never shoot the white pages. Every rewrite comes out on a new color — blue, pink, yellow, green. By the time anybody rolls camera it’s goldenrod. Right now was a white page.” She folds her hands back under her chin. “We’re on blue. Possibly pink.”
He laughs, and it moves her up and down on his chest, and she rides it out and waits.

“Four.” She reaches behind her own back with both hands, without hurrying and without taking her eyes off his, and the bra goes over the edge of the mattress after the jeans, and she settles her chin back on her hands as if nothing in the room has changed. “Visual aids.”

He has seen this much of her once before, Thursday, in the dark, in a hurry. Not like this: lit from one side by what’s left of the lights, in nothing but black cotton and the braided anklet, chin on her hands in the middle of his chest, making a point. Her face says she knows exactly what it’s doing to his side of the argument. She gives him a good long while to find that out before she goes on.

“Dailies. Thursday, on this mattress, you said, and I’m quoting, *I’ve wanted you since the window seat.*” She lays one finger flat on his chest. “And at a quarter past four you told me it isn’t me you don’t trust. It’s you. So I took a meeting with you. Three weeks of notes. You pushed my car in Buellton. You stood in my rain. You’ve been in my bed twice and you’re still wearing a belt.” She tips her head. “Jack. You are the most trustworthy man who has ever been underneath me.”
“That’s a pitch.”
“It’s *coverage*.”

It’s a good argument. Most of it is better than good. He can’t find the hole in it from underneath her, and that may be why she made it from up there, and she’s funny, and he’s laughing and he wants her and the two have got into each other and won’t come apart.

“So the notes are in,” Skye says. “The sentence doesn’t work. We’re on new pages.” She smiles down at him, slow, and her hand goes down between them to his belt, sure of itself, the way it went Thursday — and this time she says it out loud, like somebody who has made her case. “Is it still right now?”

s07b.slug: FRIDAY · 11:50 PM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: She doesn’t argue the point she just lost. Her hand comes off his belt and goes back to where it was before it went looking for the buckle — flat on his chest, over his heart — and stays there.
“A no’s a no. For tonight. For that.” She smiles when she says it, pleased with him, as if he has handed her a hard note and she likes it — and she doesn’t stop.

She goes back to where they were before her hand went to the belt, and picks it up from there. What came off for the argument stays off — the jeans on the floor with the scripts, the bra on the far side of the mattress. Nothing more does.

She’s easy in it — easy as she is barefoot on a gas-station floor, or walking into the Pacific in November — in nothing now but a pair of black cotton underwear and the braided anklet, and he’s still in his jeans with the belt done up. She has always been at home in her skin, and tonight there’s a great deal of it.

Her mouth on his, slow, and then not slow. She pushes her hair forward over one shoulder without looking, and it falls across both their faces and shuts out the lights, all but a red seam of them along the bottom. The window is cold on one of her shoulders and the rest of her is heat, skin to skin from her collarbone to his belt, her heart going fast against his, right on top of it. He finds the freckles that go on down over her shoulders, more than her face has, and puts his mouth on them, and she tips her head back for it and makes a sound he hasn’t heard out of her before, low, nothing like a laugh.

When she comes up on her hands to look at him there are smudges down her ribs where his fingers have been — gray, from under his nails, her own battery — and she looks down at herself in the red light and laughs. “You’re getting my car on me.” She rubs one with her thumb and makes it worse, and comes back down.
“I’m not doing anything,” she says against his throat, doing it.

She pulls the blanket up over both their heads, and under it there’s no light at all, only her, the heat of her and her breath and the salt at her hairline, and the braided anklet scratching at his shin through the denim. Her teeth find his shoulder. The muscles of her back move under his hands, and at the dip of her spine her skin has gone damp, and when he spreads his fingers there she presses back into them hard. He wants her so much it’s a sound in his ears, under the surf.

Once she stops, and lies with her forehead on his, both of them breathing like they’ve run the stairs up the bluff, and he thinks that’s the end of it. She starts again from the top, slower, with all night to do it in. Her hands are in his hair; she pulls his head back by it, not gently, to look at him in what light there is, and whatever she finds in his face makes her smile, and he feels the smile against his mouth before he sees it.
There’s nothing left to say no to. There’s only everything they were already doing, and the whole night to do it in, and she is in no hurry at all.

His breathing has gone loud in the room, louder than the surf at the foot of the bluff and the stereo three houses down. She lifts her head and laughs at him, low and delighted. “Breathe, Jack,” she says. “You’re scaring the neighbors.”

He isn’t trying to be good. For a stretch of it he isn’t trying anything. There’s her mouth, and the heat coming off her, and her hands in his hair, and his own hands on her back and her ribs and the long muscles beside her spine, places he’ll have to say out loud on Saturday. His thoughts come shorter. Her skin. Her breath. Her skin. It’s his own body that keeps leaning at the line, and the line holds anyway. It holds because he holds it, and it hurts.

response: “Water,” he says, and gets up.

There’s a bathroom at the end of the hall with a toothbrush glass on the sink. He fills it and brings it back and doesn’t drink it. He stands at her window with it and his back to her, bare to the waist, with the cold coming in under the sash and the surf down at the bottom of the bluff, and gives the cold a minute of him. She lets him have the minute.
When he turns around she’s under the blanket with it up to her chin, watching him.
“Better?”
“No.”
“Good,” Skye says, and lifts the edge of the blanket, and when he gets back in beside her in his jeans it has cooled enough to talk.

Somewhere inside the wall something goes *pop*, small and definite. The last knot of Christmas lights dies, and the line of light under the door dies with it, and three houses down the music keeps on while this house goes black from the roof to the alley. For the length of one wave there’s nothing in it but the surf.
Then her laugh in the dark, close to his ear.
“Unbelievable,” Skye says. “You converted the house.”
She finds a flashlight by feel, in one of the boots under the rack, and clicks it on and points it at the ceiling, and they lie there in the circle of it.

“Cruel’s a strong word,” Skye says. “I’m being *thorough*.”

And then she’s laughing at her own line, at him, at the state of him, and she can’t stop, and she has to roll off him onto her back to do it properly with both hands over her face, and the laugh does what his no didn’t: by the time she’s finished with it the room has come down to something he can lie next to.

s07c.slug: SATURDAY · 1:00 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM, IN THE DARK
body: By one o’clock there’s a candle going in a jelly jar on the floor and the flashlight has given up beside it. The fuse box is in the darkroom. “I’m not allowed in the darkroom,” Skye says. “House rule. Something about the light getting in.” She’s in her flannel and he’s back in his undershirt, and they sit against the wall under the dead window with the blanket over their knees, and the candle makes the room about the size of the candle.

She asks what he’s doing in four hours, and he tells her: the old Mission on Mission Street, at five. A guy from work asked him to come hear his mother sing. It’s the feast — today, now; midnight went by while the lights were still on. Our Lady of Guadalupe. At five in the morning they sing her *Las Mañanitas*, the birthday song, with a mariachi, and bank roses around her picture till you can smell them from the street.
“Why roses?”

So he tells her the part everybody knows. A hill outside Mexico City, in December, a long time ago. A man on his way to Mass, and a lady on the hill who sent him to the bishop. The bishop wanted a sign. She sent the man back up the hill for roses, in December, where nothing grows, and he carried them down in his coat, and when he opened the coat in front of the bishop the roses fell out on the floor and she was on the cloth.
Skye sits up off the wall. “Wait. Green cape? Stars all over it? Gold coming off her in spikes?”
“That’s her.”

“She’s on every taco truck in the Valley. She’s on the tall candles at the liquor store on Ventura. There’s a wall of her on Lankershim by a car wash, twenty feet high.” She looks at him across the candle. “I thought she was a *brand*.”
“She’s Our Lady.”
“Our Lady of what, exactly?”
“Guadalupe. It’s a place.”
“Of course she has a location,” Skye says.
“Who painted her?”
“No one. That’s the story.”

She sits with that longer than he expects, chin on her knees. “The bishop’s the only one in it I believe,” she says at last. “Somebody pitches him a miracle and he asks to see it on tape.” She tips her head back against the wall. “Whoever she is, she’s very well photographed.”
“That’s the idea,” Jack says.
“I’ll drive you,” she says. “Mission’s on my way to the freeway. I want to see the candles from the car.” And then, in the same breath: “When do you tell your priest about me?”
“This afternoon. Three-thirty.”

“Do you get points for tonight?” She puts up a hand to stop him answering, drops her voice down into her chest and flattens every vowel in it, and she’s a patient man from Ohio explaining something in a parked car: “It doesn’t work like points.”
“It doesn’t.”
“I heard you the first time.” She reaches over and turns the jar so the flame stands up straight. “Tell him I was respectful.”

Then she wants the birthday song. He knows the tune and a few words of it, and she makes him hum the rest while she puts Spanish to it, none of it Spanish and all of it confident — a verse about a dishwasher, a verse about a Saab, a verse about a priest who *requests* — until he has to put his face in the blanket. “They sing it under her window before she’s awake,” he says, when he can. “So she wakes up to it.” Skye stops. “Somebody does that for her. Every year.” “Every year.” “And she doesn’t have to do anything,” she says. “She just gets sung to.” She pulls the blanket up to her chin and watches the candle for a while with that.
A little before three he asks her to set her alarm for half past four.
“Why?”
“So I’d leave.”

She looks at him a while. Then she fishes the white iPhone out of the boot where it lives and sets the alarm, and lays it on the floor by the candle, and goes back to the story she was in the middle of — a hamburger commercial she shot at twelve in a field in Simi Valley, in a hoopskirt, which she still won’t explain.

Somewhere after half past three he falls asleep sitting up against the wall. The marimba goes at four-thirty, bright and idiotic in the dark, and when he opens his eyes she’s where she was, the blanket pulled up, the candle down in its own wax, looking at him.
“You fold your hands,” she says. “When you sleep. I watched you since half past three. You look like a knight on a tomb.”

body: She puts the top up for the cold. The canvas comes over them stiff with damp and latches at the windshield, the heater runs full blast, her bare feet on the pedals, cold or not, and Mission Street at ten to five is wet black asphalt with the signals going through their colors down the grade toward the harbor and not a car to stop.
At the light by the Greyhound depot he switches the RAZR on. It finds a bar and buzzes once in his hand.
