body: It sits on the outer screen, four hours old. He shuts the phone on it and puts it in the Carhartt. Skye downshifts for the light.

She pulls in at the curb two blocks short, by the depot bench under its caged tube of light. From there the Mission is up the street on the far side with every one of its doors open, and the doors are full of light — candles, a great many of them, and behind the candles a red that has to be roses, banked so deep the color carries two blocks. People are going in out of the dark in coats. Somewhere inside a trumpet tries a note and thinks better of it.
“That’s her?”
“That’s her.”
Skye looks with both hands on the wheel and the heater going, her face lit faintly from up the street.
“Is it rude? Watching from the car?”
“People watch her from the back all the time. She doesn’t mind.”
Skye takes that in, and nods at the doors, once, as if to somebody across a room she’s been introduced to.
“It’s yours,” she says. “I’ll watch the light come up from the freeway.”
She kisses him once, across the gearshift, her hand on the back of his neck, warm from the heater.
“Cassidy has a Saturday,” she says against his mouth. “There’s a Santa involved. Don’t ask.”
He gets out into the cold and walks the two blocks up toward the open doors with his hands in the Carhartt, and inside the trumpet starts over, for real this time.

s09.slug: SATURDAY · 5:00 AM · OLD MISSION NUESTRA SEÑORA DEL MAR, MISSION STREET
body: Every door in the long white front of the Mission is open, and the light comes out of them onto Mission Street gold and unsteady, from more candles than Jack has ever seen in one place: tall glass ones with saints painted on them, along the sills, up the steps, in rows at the foot of the walls. Down the grade toward the harbor the town is still black. Families go up the steps out of the dark in coats and blankets, grandmothers on their sons’ arms, little kids in pajama pants under their parkas, carrying roses upright in their fists with the stems wrapped in wet paper towel.

Inside it’s standing room. At the head of the aisle, on an easel under a canopy of gold cloth, Our Lady of Guadalupe stands in her starred mantle with the sunburst all around her, and the roses are banked up to her hem — in buckets, in coffee cans wrapped in foil, loose in heaps on the altar steps — so red in the candlelight they’re nearly black. Under the choir loft a mariachi in black charro suits with silver down the legs is tuning in the cold that comes in the doors: two trumpets, three violins, a guitar, and a bass guitar with a belly on it like a wine barrel. On a card table just inside, under a sign lettered in marker — CHAMPURRADO · TAMALES · GRATIS — two women are ladling something thick and chocolate-dark out of a stockpot into paper cups and handing tamales out of a cooler.

Rudy is halfway up on the left in a white shirt buttoned to the collar, his hair still wet from the comb, beside a small woman in a gray rebozo with her hands folded on the back of the pew in front. On Tuesday, over the Hobart’s steam, Rudy asked him: *Saturday, five in the morning, the Mission. My mother’s coming up from Oxnard. Come hear her sing.* Rudy sees him at the door and lifts his chin. His mother’s eyes are already shut, though nobody is singing yet.

An old man in a straw hat is coming up the center aisle on his knees, slowly, with the hat held flat against his chest, and the standing room steps out of his way and closes again behind him. Jack genuflects at the back, on stone gone slick with everybody’s wet shoes, and doesn’t know what to say to the Lady at the head of the aisle, so he says the Hail Mary, which is what it’s for.
In the last pew, in a black overcoat with the collar showing at his throat, a long way from his own altar, Father Osei lifts a hand to Jack and goes back to the hymn sheet.

Lena is at the end of a pew by the side aisle, in her coat, with the black lace mantilla over her hair. Julian is beside her with a cup of champurrado held under his chin for the warmth, leaning out over the end of the pew to ask the man with the big bass guitar something about his tuning pegs, and the man is showing him, one peg at a time. Julian looks up from the pegs and lifts his cup to Jack, glad to see him, as he is glad to see anybody. Lena turns when Jack comes in off the street alone. She takes in the hour, and the jacket he had on at the party.
“You’re up early, Youngstown.”

journal.title: Rudy (the Anchor)
journal.text: Line cook. Rosary on his wrist, a ballgame on the radio, Louis L’Amour in his apron. Did six years at Soledad. His mother came every other Sunday — three buses from Oxnard. Says: write him, even when there’s nothing to say. I told him about Rafi’s errand like a joke. ‘I know what an errand is, mijo.’ Opened the walk-in on me Tuesday. ‘Mijo. Lettuce.’ Took the lettuce himself. Tuesday, over the Hobart: come hear my mother sing at the Mission, Saturday, five a.m. She came up from Oxnard for the Virgin and sang every verse with her eyes shut.

s09a.slug: SATURDAY · 5:40 AM · OLD MISSION, THE COURTYARD
body: By twenty to six the overflow has eased the three of them out through the doors, and the mariachi has come out onto the top step so the courtyard can have the song too, with the doors open behind them on the candles and the roses and the people kneeling on the stone. *Estas son las mañanitas*, the trumpets begin, and the courtyard takes it up in Spanish — the birthday song, the one you sing under somebody’s window before they’re awake. The cold comes up out of the flagstones through the soles of Jack’s shoes.

Rudy has brought his mother out onto the steps on his arm, and she sings every verse of it with her eyes shut. Her voice comes up out of the crowd thin and certain and a little sharp, over the violins. By the sound of it she has sung this every December of her life, and she isn’t about to start reading the words now. Rudy doesn’t sing. He stands a step below her with his hands behind his back and his head down, and leaves the song to her.

Lena sings it in Spanish with the families, badly, with her whole heart, getting maybe a third of it right and singing the rest anyway. Beside her Julian has nothing to read off, no sheet and no shoulder, and by the second verse he has the tune, every turn of it, by ear, and is singing it under her in his easy baritone, a hair behind the words. Through the open doors Jack can see Father Osei in his pew, singing too, loudly, a little behind everybody and well off the note.
Over the harbor the dark has started, barely, to come apart from the hills.

Afterward the courtyard fills with steam and paper cups. Julian goes back to the card table for tamales, because the woman ladling called him *mijo* and he can’t get over it. Lena stands with Jack by the dry fountain with her champurrado and watches the doors.
“Everybody tells the roses,” she says, low. “Mama tells the roses. The nuns at the Rosary did the roses every December on a flannel board. I like the part before.”

“He was supposed to go back up the hill and see her. He said he would. And his uncle got sick — the fever that was killing everybody that year — so he stayed home and nursed him, and missed her. And then the uncle was dying, and Juan Diego went running for a priest in the dark, and he got to the hill, and he was late, and he was ashamed he hadn’t come back like he promised.” She turns her cup by the rim. “So he took the long way around. The far side of the hill. So she wouldn’t see him go by.”
On the steps the trumpets start another verse for the people still coming in off the street.

“And she came down the hill anyway,” Lena says. “Stood in his road.” She points with the cup at the banner over the doors, a bedsheet lettered by hand in red paint, the last words crowded together where whoever painted it ran short of sheet: ¿NO ESTOY YO AQUÍ, QUE SOY TU MADRE?

“*Am I not here? I, who am your mother?*” She drinks. “That’s what she said to a man taking the long way around. Then she told him his uncle was already well, and sent him up the hill for the roses. Everybody skips straight to the roses.”
The champurrado has gone cold in Jack’s hand, and the hand has started, very slightly, to shake, so he sets the cup down on the lip of the fountain and puts the hand in his pocket.
Julian comes back across the flagstones with three tamales on a paper plate. “Did you know the guitarrón has six strings,” he says, “and he tunes it by *ear*?”

On his way down the steps Rudy steers his mother past the fountain on his arm, and lifts his chin at Jack, and Julian, with a tamale halfway to his mouth, watches her go by. “Who’s the singer?” “Rudy, from the Anchor,” Jack says. “His mother.” Julian says *oh* as if somebody had told him the name of a key.

Lena takes a tamale and peels the husk back with her thumbs and tells him she did know, and Julian says somebody might have told *him*, and over the courtyard the Mission’s bell starts in for the six o’clock.

s10.slug: SATURDAY · 3:35 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE CONFESSION LINE
body: At twenty-five to four the sun is low over Las Olas and comes in sideways through the blue panes of St. Brendan’s, and lays a long blue light down the side aisle and over six folding chairs set in a row outside the coat closet. On the closet door, in capitals, on an index card: KNOCK (GENTLY). Mrs. Fitch has a card table beside it with the crossword and a plate of lemon bars under plastic wrap, and she is herself again — recovered from the punch, she tells the grandmother at the head of the line, by the grace of God and two aspirin.
Jack slept from seven to three in the Carhartt, and came across Ocean Road with his hair still flat on one side.

The line is short for the Saturday before Gaudete: the grandmother at the head of it, with wooden rosary beads the size of chickpeas; a graduate student in a Cal sweatshirt reading something with footnotes; a Newman freshman Jack knows by face, working down an examination of conscience off a laminated card and wincing at intervals. Now and then, through the closet door, comes the low sound of Father Osei’s voice, too low for words, which is what the door is for.
Lena is three chairs ahead, and turns around at the sound of the side door. “Jack.” He sits.
“Miss Broussard,” Mrs. Fitch says, filling in a word. “Your roommate is not welcome at the Epiphany party.”
“She’ll be devastated, Mrs. Fitch. She’ll wear black.”
“She wore black to *this* one. I had three cups.” Mrs. Fitch erases something, hard. “I sang a descant over Gus for an hour and told him he was dragging. He was. That is not the point.”

Halfway through the wait the 8-Ball comes out of Lena’s pocket. She shuts her eyes and holds it to her chest and asks it, under her breath but not far enough under, “Will I get a decade?” She shakes it once and turns it up to the blue light. *Signs point to yes.*
Mrs. Fitch, with her pencil on fourteen down: “Not in line, Miss Broussard.”
“Yes, ma’am.” It goes back in the pocket. “It’s for my examination of conscience,” Lena tells the freshman with the laminated card, who has looked up. “It’s more honest than the card.”
The freshman looks at his card.

At three forty-one the RAZR goes off inside the Carhartt, against his ribs — twice, short, the double buzz of a picture message. He tips the phone up out of the pocket far enough to see the outer screen: the little envelope. He doesn’t open it.
“Nor you, Mr. Costigan,” says Mrs. Fitch.
His hand goes over the pocket and keeps it there.

Lena’s eyes go to the hand. They stay on it while the closet door opens and the grandmother comes out, tucking the wooden beads into her purse with her face carefully arranged, and then they go to the door, and it’s her turn. She knocks, gently, and goes in.

She’s in there six minutes by the clock over the choir loft. When she comes out she’s pink around the eyes and very straight in the back, and she goes past the line to the Marian shrine in the side aisle, and puts a folded dollar in the box, and lights a votive off one that’s already burning, and kneels on the step in front of the rack with her hands folded on the rail.
Mrs. Fitch slides the plate of lemon bars along the card table toward him, plastic wrap and all. “For after, Mr. Costigan.”
The closet door is standing open. It’s his turn.

choices.key: On Saturday you went into the box and told Father Osei about a week of her, and the door you left open.
On Saturday, with her picture in your pocket, you stepped out of the confession line.

body: He knocks — gently; the card is very clear — and goes in.

The coat closet hasn’t changed in a week. The kneeler on this side, the folding chair on the other, the linen screen in the middle on its wooden frame with the purple of a stole showing through; the coat hooks from 1962 along the back wall; the Prodigal Son thumbtacked inside the door at the height of a kneeling man’s eyes. On the far side the chair takes the priest’s weight, and the bad leg gets itself arranged, and after that there’s nothing to hear but Mrs. Fitch’s pencil out at the card table, and that only because he’s listening for it.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.”
“It’s been a week since my last confession.”
He had it in order out there. In here it comes the way it wants to.

“You told me to change the hour,” he says. “To keep her in the daylight. I did, once. Thursday afternoon. The harbor, a man hosing down a boat, her sitting on the back of her car with a sleeve of pencils. It was easy.” There’s still black in the creases of his knuckles from a battery in Buellton, and he looks at that. “Then it got dark.”
Osei waits.

“Thursday night I went to her house. Her room. I knew what I was going there for.” He keeps his voice down, though there’s no need. “And I said no. And it stopped. Every other time it was something else that stopped it — her phone, a fire alarm, somebody knocking on a door. Thursday it was me.”

“She didn’t understand it, at first. She was afraid I thought less of her. Because of what she’d wanted.” He has the words she used and leaves them where they are. “So I told her I didn’t. And then she asked me why I’d said no, and I told her that too, and then she asked me everything. Till four in the morning. What a mortal sin is. Whether the nuns told the boys the same thing. What I say to you in here.” Something close to a laugh gets out of him. “She wanted every answer. She kept them all.”
“And she heard you?”
“She heard all of it. She argued with half of it. Then she went and made tea and came back with more questions.”
“On her porch I asked her for daylight. She said Sunday, first light, at Ellery. She’s going to teach me to surf.”
“And I told her —” This is the one. “I told her I’m not saying it’s always going to be no. Not until — I didn’t promise her that. I said it’s a no right now. She said she could work with that.”

“Last night she argued me out of it. Nearly.” He makes himself say the rest in order. “She took the sentence apart. The whole thing, point by point. She was funny, and she was right about half of it, and then she asked me if it was still right now. I said it was. I said no again.”
“And she stopped there. Only there. Whatever we’d been doing before she reached for my belt, she went back to, and kept on with it, all night.”

body: The rest of the week comes after that, a piece at a time.
“Monday there was a trailer door. She was leaving, and I caught her wrist.”
“She sent me a picture. I kept it. And what I said back.”

body.text: “I’ve lied to people about where I go.”
“I lied to her, too. Something small, about who ended up with a present.”
“And the rest of the week,” he says, and that’s as far as it goes. Osei lets it stand.

body: “I keep putting myself in the near occasion,” Jack says, in the old words, because they are still the right ones.
Osei is quiet. When he speaks it’s with the dull question first.
“Thursday night,” he says. “Did you go to her, or did she come for you?”
“I called her.”
“Why that night?”
“I heard a song.”
“Whose song?”
“Somebody else’s.”

And then, because it isn’t the whole of the answer and he’s in the one room where he can’t leave it there: “But that isn’t why I go.” It comes out faster than he meant. “It made it that night. It isn’t why. I’d have gone anyway. I go because I want to be there, Father. I like her. I like being with her.” He has run out of the right words and goes on with the ones he’s got. “She wants to know how everything works. Why I think what I think — she takes it apart and puts it back and hands it to me. She makes me laugh till it hurts. She’s good at things I’ve never tried and she makes me try them. I want to know all of her. That’s the truth. She isn’t somewhere I go to feel better.”
On the other side of the screen the priest is quiet for a while. When he speaks again his voice has changed.
“I believe you,” Osei says. “I have heard a great many young men describe a girl in here, my friend. Some of them describe a medicine. Some of them describe an alibi. You have described a person.”

“You told me she was frightened of what you thought of her, and you told her the truth. A girl who asked you everything — and you stopped it yourself, with no telephone and no alarm, and then you stayed.” On the far side the chair creaks as he shifts the bad leg. “And then you asked her for daylight, and she said yes. I prescribe daylight, and the patient books an appointment at first light, in December, in the sea. Go. Fall off the board. Fall off it many times. It is a very good hour to be bad at something.”

“Saint Thomas says that to love is to will the good of the other. Not to want her — you want her; you have told me so, and I believe that too. To *will her good*. Everything you have said to me this afternoon is a young man willing a girl’s good, and delighting in her while he does it. That is real. It is good, and it comes from God, and I want you to hear me say so before I say anything else.”
A breath, on the far side of the linen.

“And that is exactly why it is dangerous. Nobody is tempted by a thing that is only bad. A man does not risk his soul over a girl he doesn’t care for, or over a girl he could simply leave. The occasion is near because what is in it is good — and the better it is, the nearer it comes.”

“Now,” he says, gently. “The door. Telling her the truth about yourself was not a sin. You were honest about your weakness, and that is rarer than you think. But a no that is only for tonight has to be said again tomorrow night, and the night after, to a woman who heard you the first time.”
He waits until Jack has heard all of it.
“Can you?”

choices.key: Father Osei asked if you can say no every night to a woman who heard you the first time. You said you’ll say it every night.
response: “Then I’ll say it every night,” Jack says.
“Then say it before you get in the car,” Osei says. “Not after. Before, it is still yours to say.”

“For your penance, a decade for her. By her name,” Osei says. “And with every one, ask God for her good — the thing you already want for her. Ask it plainly, so you hear what it is.” A pause. “And one Hail Mary for whoever wrote the song.”
Jack says the Act of Contrition. He has been saying it since he was seven. Today it catches on *firmly resolve*, and he goes back for the words and says them again, slower.
Osei’s hand comes up.

“God, the Father of mercies, through the death and resurrection of his Son has reconciled the world to himself and sent the Holy Spirit among us for the forgiveness of sins; through the ministry of the Church may God give you pardon and peace, and I absolve you from your sins in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.”
“Amen.”
“The Lord has freed you from your sins. Go in peace.”

While he was in there the blue panes have climbed off the pews and gone up the far wall, thinner. He kneels in the back pew under what’s left of them and breathes to the bottom of his lungs, for the first time since Thursday.
He prays the decade on his knuckles, ten times round, with her name at the front of every one. *Skye.* The extra one he says for Julian, by name, because the priest didn’t have it to give him.

s10b.slug: SATURDAY · 4:45 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE COURTYARD
body: He got up off the folding chair at ten to four, when it was his turn, and Mrs. Fitch said it to her crossword as he went past the card table: “Father keeps a chair warm for the ones who come back, Mr. Costigan.”

He didn’t go far. The low wall under the olive tree is fifty feet from the side door, and he has been on it most of an hour with the RAZR shut in his hand. The outer screen has its envelope. He hasn’t opened it. The wind came around cold off the water at noon and hasn’t let up; it goes through the olive tree in gusts and turns the leaves silver side up, and the sun is down on the roofs of Las Olas, gold, nearly gone. Across Ocean Road the windows of Delgado have started coming on, one floor at a time.
At twenty past four Lena came out the side door in her coat, done with her prayers, and saw him on the wall. She lifted a hand. He lifted his. She went on down the path to Ocean Road.

Now the five o’clock is coming across the courtyard: a man carrying a girl asleep on his shoulder, two grandmothers arm in arm against the wind, a boy in a clip-on tie being steered by the collar. Inside, the closet door will be standing open on nobody.

Father Osei comes out of Newman House in rubber boots, with a pipe wrench the length of his forearm. He gets down — slowly; the leg — beside the valve box set in the dirt at the foot of the wall, and holds the wrench out to Jack. “Hold this.”

Jack holds it. Osei lifts the iron lid off the box and clears a winter of olive leaves out of it with his bare hand, and a snail, which he sets on top of the wall. They fit the jaws to the valve together, and Jack leans on the handle, and Osei puts his own hands over Jack’s and leans too. The valve doesn’t move. They try it the other way, in case. It doesn’t move that way either. The sprinkler head stands up out of the mud as it has since November.
“Brass, 1962,” Osei says. “Installed by an optimist. I try it every Saturday after the line. It is good for my humility, and for nothing else.”
Osei sits down on the wall beside him to rest the leg, and breathes, and looks at the sprinkler. The snail has started down the far side of the wall.
“The closet closes at a quarter to five,” he says. “My office doesn’t. I told you where the light is.”

response: “Now?”

“Now is the only time I have ever been any good at.” He takes the wrench back and gets up off the wall, and goes ahead of Jack across the courtyard toward Newman House, slowly, the bad leg setting the pace, against the families going the other way into church.

body: The office is the one Jack remembers from September: the stethoscope on its hook by the window, the chessboard on the side table with a game still standing on it and the white bishop with the chip out of its shoulder, and highlife on the record player, guitars and a horn line going round like a wheel. Osei lifts the needle off in the middle of the song, and the room goes quiet enough to hear the courtyard.

He lays the pipe wrench across the desk blotter and doesn’t bother with the rubber boots. Out of his cardigan pocket he takes a purple stole, kisses it, and puts it on over the cardigan. He pulls the second chair out from the wall and sets it beside his own, both of them facing the crucifix on the far wall instead of each other.
“Face to face is permitted,” he says, lowering himself into the one on the left, the bad leg last. “Side by side is easier on everybody.”

Past the window the families are going in to the five o’clock in their coats. “They will start without me,” Osei says. “Mrs. Fitch will give them a rosary. They like it when I am late. It makes them feel holy.”
Jack sits down beside him. The crucifix has them both.
“Bless me, Father, for I have sinned.”
“It’s been a week since my last confession.”
He had it in order out there. In here it comes the way it wants to.

“You told me to change the hour,” he says. “To keep her in the daylight. I did, once. Thursday afternoon. The harbor, a man hosing down a boat, her sitting on the back of her car with a sleeve of pencils. It was easy.” There’s still black in the creases of his knuckles from a battery in Buellton, and he looks at that. “Then it got dark.”
Osei waits.

“Thursday night I went to her house. Her room. I knew what I was going there for.” He keeps his voice down, though there’s no need. “And I said no. And it stopped. Every other time it was something else that stopped it — her phone, a fire alarm, somebody knocking on a door. Thursday it was me.”

“She didn’t understand it, at first. She was afraid I thought less of her. Because of what she’d wanted.” He has the words she used and leaves them where they are. “So I told her I didn’t. And then she asked me why I’d said no, and I told her that too, and then she asked me everything. Till four in the morning. What a mortal sin is. Whether the nuns told the boys the same thing. What I say to you in here.” Something close to a laugh gets out of him. “She wanted every answer. She kept them all.”
“And she heard you?”
“She heard all of it. She argued with half of it. Then she went and made tea and came back with more questions.”
“On her porch I asked her for daylight. She said Sunday, first light, at Ellery. She’s going to teach me to surf.”
“And I told her —” This is the one. “I told her I’m not saying it’s always going to be no. Not until — I didn’t promise her that. I said it’s a no right now. She said she could work with that.”

“Last night she argued me out of it. Nearly.” He makes himself say the rest in order. “She took the sentence apart. The whole thing, point by point. She was funny, and she was right about half of it, and then she asked me if it was still right now. I said it was. I said no again.”
“And she stopped there. Only there. Whatever we’d been doing before she reached for my belt, she went back to, and kept on with it, all night.”

Osei is quiet. When he speaks it’s with the dull question first.
“Thursday night,” he says. “Did you go to her, or did she come for you?”
“I called her.”
“Why that night?”
“I heard a song.”
“Whose song?”
“Somebody else’s.”

And then, because it isn’t the whole of the answer and he’s in the one room where he can’t leave it there: “But that isn’t why I go.” It comes out faster than he meant. “It made it that night. It isn’t why. I’d have gone anyway. I go because I want to be there, Father. I like her. I like being with her.” He has run out of the right words and goes on with the ones he’s got. “She wants to know how everything works. Why I think what I think — she takes it apart and puts it back and hands it to me. She makes me laugh till it hurts. She’s good at things I’ve never tried and she makes me try them. I want to know all of her. That’s the truth. She isn’t somewhere I go to feel better.”
Beside him the priest is quiet for a while, looking at the crucifix. When he speaks again his voice has changed.
“I believe you,” Osei says. “I have heard a great many young men describe a girl to me, my friend. Some of them describe a medicine. Some of them describe an alibi. You have described a person.”

“You told me she was frightened of what you thought of her, and you told her the truth. A girl who asked you everything — and you stopped it yourself, with no telephone and no alarm, and then you stayed.” Osei shifts the bad leg. “And then you asked her for daylight, and she said yes. I prescribe daylight, and the patient books an appointment at first light, in December, in the sea. Go. Fall off the board. Fall off it many times. It is a very good hour to be bad at something.”

“Saint Thomas says that to love is to will the good of the other. Not to want her — you want her; you have told me so, and I believe that too. To *will her good*. Everything you have said to me this afternoon is a young man willing a girl’s good, and delighting in her while he does it. That is real. It is good, and it comes from God, and I want you to hear me say so before I say anything else.”
A breath, from the chair on his left.

“And that is exactly why it is dangerous. Nobody is tempted by a thing that is only bad. A man does not risk his soul over a girl he doesn’t care for, or over a girl he could simply leave. The occasion is near because what is in it is good — and the better it is, the nearer it comes.”

“Now,” he says, gently. “The door. Telling her the truth about yourself was not a sin. You were honest about your weakness, and that is rarer than you think. But a no that is only for tonight has to be said again tomorrow night, and the night after, to a woman who heard you the first time.”
He waits until Jack has heard all of it.
“Can you?”

response: “Then I’ll say it every night,” Jack says.

“Amen.”

Jack sits down on his bed in his jacket. His right hand is in the pocket of it, and has been since Ocean Road.

“You have mail,” Theo says, without turning around. “I didn’t read it. I read who it’s from and who else it’s to. Postmen are allowed that much.” He tips the screen a few degrees toward the room. “Miss Broussard is on the To: line. Hale doesn’t BCC. It’s the most attractive thing about him.”
Jack gets up and reads it over his shoulder.

body.text:
Received, both. Mr. Costigan at 12:14 today, Miss Broussard at seven on Thursday morning, in Latin, for reasons she will no doubt explain. I am not surprised and I am not disappointed, which at my age is the same thing as joy.

Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are.

body: Hale sent it yesterday at two minutes past five. Jack would very much like to see the Latin.

Theo waits until he’s finished. “‘The same thing as joy,’” he says. “I want that on my headstone. Under the name, in a smaller font.” He scrolls. “You slept from seven till three in your jacket,” he says. “I tiptoed. It was very moving. I’ve never tiptoed for anyone.”
“You could have woken me up.”
“I considered it. It seemed unsporting. You were in a jacket.”
Theo goes back to the screen. “She knocked last night,” he says. “Twelve-thirty. I said the library.”
“She told me.”
“Of course she did.”

“Thanks.”
“Don’t. I lied to a woman in a cardigan at half past twelve. It goes on the tab.”
Jack goes back and sits on his own bed. Down the hall the orchestra comes up again, and the applause with it, for somebody in New York.
Theo swivels the desk chair round to face the room, for the first time since Jack came in, and considers the pocket of Jack’s jacket.
“Your pocket has been looking at me since you came in, Costigan.”
Jack takes his hand out of it. The pocket goes on being a pocket.
“The stairwell has a bar,” Theo says, and turns back around to the lamp. “Go and be private somewhere with reception.”

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are.

The jukebox by the door has been playing whatever the Saturday room fed it since seven — Patsy Cline twice, the one Mariah Carey somebody always picks, then nothing for twenty minutes — and at twenty to twelve it takes a quarter and gives back Dusty Springfield, low and sure of herself, singing about a preacher’s boy who could talk her into anything.

The room is down to the people who meant to stay. Merle and a man off his boat at the far end of the counter, in their boots. A trucker in the booth by the window, working through a chicken-fried steak with the sports page folded beside it. In the corner booth a couple from the college with one plate of fries and two forks, building a lake of ketchup together. The Hobart hisses through a cycle. From the sink Jack can see the length of the counter through the pass.

She came in out of the cold with the door still swinging behind her and went to the jukebox before she looked for a seat, and now she’s on the third stool from the register, turning a little on it to the song, in a man’s flannel buttoned to the throat and a gray knit cap pulled down to her eyebrows, her cheeks red from three hours of an open top on the 101. She finds him through the pass. At the throat of the flannel, under the top button, there’s a second collar, blue, button-down, and he knows it from across the room.

body.text: He leans out through the pass with a rack of cups. “Did you look?” she says. “Not yet.” “Good.” She undoes the top button of the flannel, just the one, and the blue collar comes out over it. Enough.
He leans out through the pass with a rack of cups, and she taps the blue collar once with one finger, and goes back to the song.
He leans out through the pass with a rack of cups, and she taps the blue collar once with one finger. “You didn’t answer,” she says. “That’s fine. I came in person.”

body: She has found the board by the register: PIE OF THE DAY, PUMPKIN, in Gloria’s chalk, and under it on its own strip of masking tape, JACK’S RATINGS: MARIONBERRY 4/10 · OLALLIEBERRY 9/10. She reads it with her lips moving and turns back to the pass with both eyebrows up, and mouths it at him across the room: *Four?* He mouths back, *It was dry.* She puts a hand over her heart, for the marionberry.

He gets the rack into the Hobart without looking at what he’s doing, and pulls the door down, and looks again to make sure she’s still there. She is. She’s eating a creamer out of the bowl on the counter like it’s a shot.

Gloria comes out of the back with a rack of pie plates against her hip — his, still steaming from the Hobart — and bends to slide them under the counter by the register, and on the way down she gets a look at the third stool, and comes back up slower than she went. She wipes her hands down her apron and comes along the counter to it.
“You’re the girl on the boarding-school show,” Gloria says. “My granddaughter’s got you on her wall. Over the bed. With the lake.”
“That’s me,” Skye says, bright and instant, a girl answering to her name at roll call.
“In here you’re a slice of pie, hon.” Gloria takes the pencil out of her bun and holds it. “What’ll it be.”
Skye looks past her, through the pass, at the dishwasher. “Whatever he’d rate me.”
Gloria turns around and looks at Jack over the heat lamps for a long time, long enough that the sink water runs off his wrists and into his sleeves.

In the corner booth the girl has stopped building the lake. She has a hand on her boyfriend’s arm. “Oh my God,” she says, not quietly. “*Cassidy*.” Her phone is already out of her purse, a pink one that slides open, and it comes up over the fries with its little lens pointed at the third stool.
Skye turns on the stool to it with her smile already on, all of it at once, like a porch light on a timer.

choices.text: Come out from the sink. “She’s off the clock.”
response: He comes out through the swinging door with his sleeves wet to the elbow and the apron soaked down the front, and stands at the end of the counter between the third stool and the corner booth.
“She’s off the clock.”

The couple look at the dishwasher. Gloria looks at him. On the stool Skye turns away from the little lens to look at him too, at the wet apron and the rack-burned knuckles, and puts her chin in her hand to watch the rest of it.
Gloria, to the booth: “Pie or the door.”
They order pie. The phone goes back in the purse without a click.
He stays at the sink.

Gloria puts the pencil back in her bun and walks the length of the counter to the corner booth, and stands at the end of their table with her hands folded on her apron until the girl looks up from the little screen into her face.
“Pie or the door.”
They order pie. The phone goes back in the purse without a click.
“She’s my cousin from Ohio,” Jack says through the pass, loud enough for the booth.
The boy looks at the third stool — a tan in December, salt in the hair coming out from under the cap — and back at the dishwasher. “From *Ohio*?”
“Akron,” Skye says, beaming at him. “It’s very sunny. It’s a secret.”
The girl lowers the phone to think about Akron, and while she’s thinking about it Gloria arrives at the end of their table. “Pie or the door.”
They order pie. The phone goes back in the purse without a click.

s12a.slug: SATURDAY · 11:50 PM · THE ANCHOR, THE PASS → THE SINK
body: Gloria cuts it at the pass, on the steel shelf under the heat lamps, where he can watch her do it: the knife in, the server under, a wedge of boysenberry coming up out of the tin with its insides running purple onto the plate. She says it low, to the pie.
“Boysenberry.”
“What’s wrong with boysenberry?”

“Nothing, hon. It’s every berry some fella in Anaheim could get his hands on, crossed.” She wipes the server on a towel. “Sweet up front, tart after, and it stains. You’ll be getting it out from under your nails till Easter.”
She lifts the plate. And going past the pass with it, not quite low enough: “That one’s not waiting for any door.”
She sets it down in front of the third stool with a fork and no speech. Skye takes one look at the slice and laughs at Jack through the pass, delighted with it.

By midnight she has asked Gloria if she can wash a rack. “Health code,” Gloria says, and hands her a bar towel instead, and Skye moves to the end stool by the dish station and dries coffee cups as they come out of the Hobart, holding each one up to the light before she sets it down, a little stack going up beside her on the Formica. She is very bad at it and very serious about it. He keeps looking up from the sink to watch her do it, and doesn’t care who sees.

Between cups she reviews his work for Gloria, low, across the end of the counter. “He racks the saucers before the cups. Is that allowed?” “It’s how I taught him.” “It’s very confident.” She holds a cup up to the light. “He has a committed wrist.” Gloria says the boy has had a committed wrist since August, and goes back down to the register, and Skye looks as pleased as if she’s been told a secret about him.
“What did she rate you?” she says, when Gloria has gone.
“Lattice-top.”
“Which is?”
“Pretty on top. Everything’s leaking underneath.”
Skye thinks about that with a cup in each hand. “She’s good,” she says.
In the window booth the trucker folds his sports page, digs a fistful of quarters out of his jacket, and goes back past the restrooms to the pay phone on the wall. Skye goes on drying.

Rudy comes down from the grill with a ramekin of flan and sets it beside her stack of cups. By the time she has her wallet out of the flannel he’s back at the flat-top. “My mother’s,” he says, scraping. “She came up from Oxnard for the Virgin. Sang at the Mission at five this morning, every verse.”
Skye points her fork down the counter at Jack. “He was there.”
“I saw him,” Rudy says, and goes back to the grill.
She eats the flan in four bites, with her eyes shut for the first one. Then, low, with the fork aimed at Gloria’s back: “Is she one of your everybody?”
“She’s the boss.”
“Then I’ve met one.” She sounds pleased about it.

Her day comes out between cups, in one breath: seven hours as Cassidy in a red velvet Santa hat on a stage of fake snow outside a toy store, in a mall in Burbank, for a network toy drive her mother booked in October; a line that went down an escalator and out into the parking structure; a man who asked her to sign his little girl’s cast, and then held out his own arm.
“Did you sign it?”
“I signed the cast. I told him the arm was a union thing.” She holds a cup up to the light and finds a spot on it and goes after the spot. “Did you tell him?”

body.text: “Yes.” “Everything?” “Everything.” She dries the cup slowly, all the way around. “Am I famous in there?” “Nobody’s famous in there.” She holds the cup up to the light and keeps it there. “I’d like that room,” she says, and puts it on the stack.
body.else: “Not yet.” She turns the cup once inside the towel and sets it on the stack.

body: At 11:52 the RAZR goes against his hip under the apron. He dries a hand on his jeans and reads it at the drainboard, with his back to the room.

body.text: Ingram by 28 points. Remy is inconsolable. Pie? —L.

body: The window over the sink is black, and the counter is in it behind him: the stools, the pie case, and her on the end one with the towel gone still in her hands, watching his back. When he turns around she is drying the same cup. Past her, in the glass, Gloria at the register is looking from his back to the end stool, and goes on wiping the pie case with a rag.

journal.title: Gloria (the Anchor)
journal.text: Hired me for rating her pie a four. Rated me a lattice-top. I’m not going to ask. Told her I won’t be the next guy at the door. She says nobody holds a door that long without somebody else walking through it. Asked after the pecan. I said she’s seeing somebody, he’s nice. She said lattice-top. Boxed a pie for Nonna. From a woman who’s been on her feet thirty years. Peach is August. St. Nicholas Eve, at the end of my shift, low, at the pass: ‘Pecan came to see if you were here.’ Gave my Thursday to Hector — his girl’s due at Christmas. ‘Don’t argue with a baby.’ Says I look like the pie case at closing. Rated somebody new. Boysenberry. ‘That one’s not waiting for any door.’

journal.title: The Anchor
journal.text: Marionberry: 4/10. Olallieberry: 9/10 — Dad would eat two pieces and complain about the second. Gloria rated Lena: pecan. She rated Margot without meeting her: rhubarb — tart, and nobody can decide if it’s a fruit. She rated Becca without meeting her: apple. Honest crust. Nobody loses sleep over an apple. Then she asked what happened to the pecan. A whole pie for a funeral is half price. I work here Tue/Thu/Sat, seven to one. Once a year the kitchen goes dark on a Thursday. Saturday the 10th Gloria met Becca: ‘Apple. Told you, hon.’ She looked at Wes a long time. ‘Peach.’ Everybody likes a peach, she says. Saturday the 12th: boysenberry, for a girl off the TV. Sweet up front, tart after. It stains.

s13.slug: SUNDAY · 1:05 AM · THE WHARF → THE SAAB
body: The wind has been at the sky since dark and scrubbed it down to the stars, more of them than Marisol usually admits to, and it comes along the wharf off the water hard enough to lean on. The bait shack is shut up, its cooler humming behind the plywood. Under the last lamp before it the Saab sits with its top down in the cold, on principle.

She walks beside him with the white clamshell held flat on both palms like a cake on its way to a party, in the knit cap and his shirt and her flannel over that, and the water slaps at the pilings under the planks and goes back out. Halfway along she gives him the box, and puts both her hands inside his jacket against his ribs, and walks the rest of the way like that, sideways, steering him by them.
“Boysenberry,” she says. “She never told me what it means.”
“It’s a cross. Some guy in Anaheim crossed every berry he could get.”
“And?”
“It stains.”
Skye looks down at the box. “Good,” she says.
At the car he sets the box on the hood, and she turns around with her back against the door and her hands in the flannel pockets, and looks up at him under the lamp.
“It’s Sunday now,” she says. “New day.” She tips her head. “Is it still right now?”
“It’s still right now.”
She nods, as though he has confirmed a booking. “I’m going to ask every day,” Skye says. “It’s on my call sheet.”
“Every day.”
“Every single one. And one night you’ll be tired, or it’ll be raining, or the Browns will have lost —”
“They won Thursday.”
“I looked it up. Two and eleven.” She smiles up at him under the lamp, entirely at her ease. “I like my odds.”
“Six-thirty,” she says. “Ellery. You asked for daylight. I’m giving you December’s.”
She takes one hand out of her pocket and gets hold of his jacket by the zipper. “Or,” she says. “Come home with me. Just sleep. I’ve never tried it.”
“Sleeping,” she says, when he looks at her. “I know what it sounds like. I mean the word.”

body.text: Before he gets in the car he says it: “Whatever we do. No.” She laughs up at him, delighted, with her hand still on his zipper. “You’re doing it in advance now,” she says. “That’s new.”

choices.text: Go home with her. Just sleep.
choices.key: At one in the morning on the wharf she said she’ll ask every day. Then she asked you home, to sleep. You went.
At one in the morning on the wharf she said she’ll ask every day. You went home, and met her at Ellery at first light.
response: “Six-thirty,” he says. “Ellery. Daylight.”
“Daylight,” Skye says, and lets go of the zipper.

She drives him up to the Marine Lab turnout with the clamshell in his lap and stops short of the chain. When he’s out she leans across the seat. “Eat that,” she says. “All of it. The water’s going to take everything you’ve got, and I want it to have to work.” She reaches over and pulls his door shut herself, and goes.

s13a.slug: SUNDAY · 1:40 AM · DEL PLAYA, HER ROOM
body: The fuse is still out. The box is in the darkroom, where she isn’t allowed, and the house is dark from the alley to the porch except for the jelly jar on her floor, which she lights with a match from a book that says THE ANCHOR on the cover. She must have taken it off the register on the way out; he didn’t see her do it.

They eat Gloria’s slice out of the clamshell on the floor by the candle, with their fingers, because the forks are downstairs in the dark. It’s still warm in the middle. It stains them both to the second knuckle, and she holds up her purple fingers in the candlelight and says, “She did warn you.”

Then the blanket. They get under it in their clothes — his jeans and his undershirt; her flannel, and his oxford under that, which she isn’t giving back — with the candle on the floor beside the mattress and the window cold over them.
“This is the sleeping way,” she says.
“I just made it up.”

She arranges them: her back to his front, his arm over her, the blanket up to her ear. “Hands where I can see them,” she says, and finds his in the dark and lays it on the outside of the flannel, over her stomach, and folds her own on top of it. “Mine too.”
Her hair is in his mouth. He leaves it there.

She talks. She tells him how it’s going to go at Ellery: how you watch a set come in from outside so you know which wave is yours; where your feet go when you stand; how he is going to want to look down at his feet and mustn’t, because the board goes where you look; how the first time you stand up, the first real time, there’s a second where — and somewhere in the middle of that second, with the sentence still open, she’s asleep.
He can tell by her breathing. It slows and drops and catches once on something and lets it go, and her hand on top of his goes heavy.

He doesn’t sleep. He lies there with her breathing against his arm and the candle burning low on the floor, and says the night prayer in his head, the short one they said at the end of every retreat at Mooney. *Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit.* And the antiphon after it, which tonight he gets the first half of and she gets the second: *Protect us, Lord, as we stay awake; watch over us as we sleep.* He puts her in it by name, and asks for what he usually asks for her.
Some time after three she talks in her sleep, distinctly and crossly, like a line she has been given too early: “Not now, Irene. Fractions later.” And goes back under.
The candle burns down to a coin of light at the bottom of the jar. At 5:40 the marimba starts up inside a boot under the rack, chirping away in the dark.

She comes up out of sleep all at once, onto one elbow, and for a second she seems not to know where she is — the black window, the strange weight of an arm across her — and he feels her go rigid against him. Then she does know.
She sits up in the blanket with her hair flat on one side and his collar crooked under the flannel, and looks at him in what’s left of the candle.
“I slept,” she says. “With somebody in the room. That doesn’t happen.” She pulls the blanket up around her shoulders and holds it shut in both fists. “I always stay up to see what they want.”
Before he can answer she’s out from under the blanket and on her knees at the rack, pulling things off hangers and dropping them on the floor in the dark, looking for a wetsuit.

Theo is asleep, or doing it well. He is a long shape under the duvet with his face to the wall, and his phone lies dark on the desk beside the lamp. Jack gets his boots off without the lamp and lies down with his hands under his head.

He smells of the Anchor’s fryer and the cold off the wharf, and a little of her. On the desk the outer screen of the RAZR says 1:31, and later 2:40, and later 3:52. Some time after three he starts a decade on his knuckles and loses count in the fourth Hail Mary and starts it over, and loses it again in the same place, and lets that be the prayer. In a few hours there’s a beach, and her, and a board he has never stood on, and lying here doesn’t bring any of it closer.

At half past five Theo gets up. He does it in the dark, without the lamp: the duvet, the closet door on its track, a sweater going over his head, a zipper. Something gets knocked off the desk and caught before it lands, and there’s a long quiet after the catch, as if he’s listening to see whether the room woke up. Nothing on his feet. He opens the door to the hall, and the light comes in along the carpet as far as the foot of Jack’s bed, and Theo stands in the doorway in it with his back to the room, and stays, long enough that Jack, lying there with his eyes shut, starts to believe he has changed his mind.
He hasn’t. He goes, barefoot, and draws the door to behind him without a sound, and his good loafers are still standing just inside it, side by side, toes to the hall.

Jack gets up and bends one slat of the blind. Down on Ocean Road, under the streetlight, Theo crosses the empty road toward the dark of the Grove with his hands in the pockets of the sweater, walking on the cold asphalt as if it were carpet, and is in the trees.

At ten to six Jack goes too. He steps around the loafers on his way out. Downstairs on the walk he laces his boots on the curb and turns east, toward the Marine Lab and the bluff, with the cold coming up through the soles and the sky over the hills not yet anything at all. Two of them out of one room before light on a Sunday, both of them going to the water, opposite ways.

journal.title: Theo, before light
journal.text: Came in barefoot at 5:20, sand and wet jeans. ‘Couldn’t sleep.’ There was a girl in our room. Sunday, Sept. 20, 6:10, wet to the shins and hay on his sweater: he says he runs now. Four miles. Barefoot. Sunday, Oct. 11, before light: wet to the shins again. He drives to where he runs. Sunday, Oct. 25, before light, at a motel above Lucia: up the path from the water, wet to the shin, sand on the cashmere. ‘Couldn’t sleep. Went to look at the ocean.’ Sunday, Nov. 1, Halloween’s morning after: asleep on his covers in the dinner jacket at seven, shoes on, sand to the knees, the hems wet. Sunday, Dec. 6, St. Nicholas: at half past five I heard him stand in the open door a long time, and go barefoot. Back at 6:40, wet to the shin and sand above it, with a gas-station coffee and his loafers in his hand. Sunday, Dec. 13: half past five, barefoot again. I went at ten to six, the other way.

body: Up on the bluff the Saab sits in the dirt turnout with its engine off, ticking as it cools, and the radio still going on what’s left of the battery: the college station, and a song that is mostly one bright figure on a keyboard going around and around while a man’s voice climbs up over it asking for almost nothing, for his girls. Skye has it turned up. Below the bluff the surf is making the long tearing sound it makes before anybody is in it.

body.text: They came out of her alley at six with two boards across the back seat and the nose of the long one standing up over the trunk lid, her hair still flat on the side where his arm was.

She was at the Marine Lab chain at six with the top down and two boards across the back seat, the nose of the long one standing up over the trunk lid, and a second wetsuit folded on his seat that he had to hold in his lap the four miles up the coast.

body: Both boards came out from under her porch. One is a fat soft-top longboard with a bite out of its rail. The other is hers, short and battered, waxed so many times the wax has gone to lumps. “The boys won’t let it on the rack,” she says. “They say it’s a menace. It’s a *personality*.”
Now he’s behind the open passenger door with a towel around his waist, losing a fight with a wetsuit.
“Whose is this?”

“Tomás’s. He’s in Baja till tonight.” She’s already in hers — a worn black 4/3 with the knees gone shiny — and she’s sitting on the fender eating a banana, watching him. “He’s bigger than you in every direction.”

He is. The legs come down past Jack’s ankles and bunch there. The sleeves swallow his hands. There’s room in the chest for a second Costigan. She gets off the fender and hauls the zipper cord up his back with one knee in his spine, and pats him twice between the shoulder blades when it’s done. “Recess,” she says.

Over the mountains the sky has started to go rose before the sun, a long band of it laid along the ridges with the dark still sitting on top. It’s Gaudete Sunday. Out on the horizon the platforms are still lit from the night. A line of pelicans goes by low over the water, single file, riding the air off the faces of the waves without a wingbeat among them, and the black stumps of her oil pier stand out into the surf in their two crooked rows.
They go down the path barefoot with the boards under their arms. The sand at the bottom is so cold it hurts.

The first wave that gets inside Tomás’s suit goes down his back and both legs at once, and the cold goes through the neoprene like news. His forehead aches at the bone. By the time he’s chest-deep in the whitewater, holding the soft-top out in front of him like a door he’s been asked to carry, he has forgotten every thought he came down the path with.

She can surf. He learns that from the whitewater. She lies down on the short board and paddles straight out into the break, and when a wave stands up in front of her she pushes the nose under and goes under with it, board and girl both, and comes up on the far side already paddling. Past the break she sits up and waits, her legs in the water, looking out to sea. Then she turns, takes three strokes, and is up — low, quick, both feet on the board in one move he doesn’t see — and she goes down the line on the face of a wave going green under her in the first light, with the spray tearing off the top of it in the wind, and rides it clear down to where it closes out by the pilings, and kicks out over the back. He’s standing in the whitewater with his mouth open. Some of the Pacific gets in.

He is terrible. He pearls: the nose goes under and the board stands up on end and throws him. He rolls, and comes up under the board instead of beside it. He eats it — a phrase she teaches him the first time he does it, with his teeth. He gets sand in his molars, salt up the back of his nose, a scrape on his chin from the rail. Tomás’s legs go on filling and draining like bilges.

She teaches. She paddles in to the whitewater and sits on her board next to him while he gets his breath, and she doesn’t make it a favor. “Paddle,” she says. “*Paddle*. Now pop. No — that’s a push-up. Up. Not up on your *knees*. You’re praying.”
“I’m not praying.”
“You’re on your knees on a board with your eyes shut.”

Once, between sets, she leans off her board and kisses him, a cold mouth and salt, the water off her hair running into his eye, and then she gets a hand on the tail of the soft-top and shoves him into the next one.
Somewhere around the tenth time he comes up spitting, he notices his face hurts. It’s the cold, and it’s the grinning. He’s been doing it since the first wipeout and hasn’t stopped.
Out past the break a bigger set is coming, three dark lines on the water with the sun just getting onto them.
“First one’s mine,” Skye says, and lies down on her board. “Second one you can have. Or you can stay in the kiddie pool.”

response: He gets the soft-top turned around and paddles at the second wave with everything he’s got, and gets up onto the shoulder of it somehow, and at the top he’s looking straight down a moving hill of green water at the sand, a long way off.

Then the hill falls on him. It holds him under long enough to think about it — sand, the leash yanking at his ankle, both of Tomás’s legs going different directions at once — and spits him out in the shallows on his back with the ocean coming out of his nose. He’s laughing before he’s got air to do it with.
Out in the lineup Skye is draped over her board, laughing too hard to paddle. When she gets enough breath back she cups her hands. “*Again!*”
“Show me again,” he says.

She slides off her board into the water beside him and puts him on the soft-top herself: hands here, under the chest, not on the rails; feet together; look at the beach, not the board. “When I say, you get up like you mean it,” she says. “Not like you’re asking.” She takes hold of the tail and looks back over her shoulder at what’s coming, and waits, and waits. “*Now* —”

She shoves. He gets up. It isn’t pretty — a crouch, knees out, arms out for two buckets nobody gave him — but it’s up, on his feet, with the board moving under him and the beach coming at him, for two seconds before the Pacific takes it back.
Behind him she’s shrieking. When he comes up she’s on her knees on her board with both arms over her head. “You *stood*! Ohio *stood*!”
“I’m a natural,” he says.

He takes the next whitewater flat on his belly with his chin on the board and his arms hugging the rails, and it carries him, foam to his ears, clear in to the sand. He gets up in four inches of water, turns around to the lineup, and takes a bow in Tomás’s sagging suit.
Out past the break Skye applauds, sitting on her board, both hands over her head, and keeps applauding until she falls off it.

s14a.slug: SUNDAY · 8:10 AM · ELLERY, THE CUT BANK
body: By ten past eight the sun is over the ridge and hasn’t warmed anything yet. The wind has come up off the water, steady and cold, and it finds every wet place on him. They’re back in the striped blanket at the top of the beach where the sand is dry, under the cut bank and its brush, the two boards stuck nose-up in the sand in front of them. He’s in his jeans and his sweatshirt again with his hair in salty spikes. His lips are blue; she tells him so twice. She has the thermos between her knees — hot chocolate from a packet — and she makes him drink first.

Then she stands up out of the blanket into the wind and unzips her wetsuit by its cord, and peels it off her arms and down to her waist, taking her time about it: a black bikini top and gooseflesh from her collarbone down. She towels her hair facing him, with the towel snapping.
It’s broad daylight on a public beach and she’s turning blue, and he looks anyway. She sees him do it and towels harder.
“This is me respecting the letter,” Skye says. “Look how respectful I’m being.”
“You’re turning blue.”
“Blue with integrity.”

She lasts another ten seconds of it, and then she pulls a sweatshirt over her head with the neck cut out of it and drops back into the blanket against him, and gets her feet in under his thigh, two blocks of ice.
She looks him over: the blue mouth, the sand in his eyebrow, the scrape on his chin from the rail. “You look like you lost a war.”
“My roommate asked me that. Friday, six in the morning.” He gets his hands around the cup. “Why I look like I just went through a warzone.”
She unscrews the cap.
“Tell him it was a peace mission,” Skye says. She pours.
“Who taught you?” he says, when he can feel his mouth again. “To do that.”

“A stunt double.” She blows on her cup. “On a sitcom I did when I was a kid — I was somebody’s little sister for a season. “What happened?”
“My mother found wax in my hair.” She hands him the cup back. “You’re not bad in the water. You’re bad on the *board*. You swim like somebody who grew up in a lake.”
“Lake Milton. And Erie. Erie has waves.”
“Erie has *opinions*,” Skye says.

“Do the lion again,” she says. “The man who loves himself anyway.” He gives her the sentence again, with no voice left and sand in his teeth, and she says it along with him under her breath, half a word behind, learning it.

Down the beach a man in a wetsuit with a gray ponytail comes down the path with a longboard on his head, and stops at the bottom to read the water, lifts his chin at the two of them in the blanket like they’re regulars, and goes on in.
“When do you go?” she says.
“Saturday. The nineteenth.”
“Six days.”
“You’re counting.”
“I don’t count,” Skye says. “I have people who count.”

body.text: She says it into the steam off her cup, and grins over it at him.
She says it with both hands around the cup, and when she’s done her thumbs go on working at the rim of it, around and around, until he puts his hand over them, and they quit.

body: “January I’ll be here every day,” she says. “You’ll be sick of me by Valentine’s.”
“Valentine’s is three days before Lent.”
“What happens at Lent?”
“You give something up.”
She looks at him over the cup. “Good luck,” Skye says.
Out past the break the man with the ponytail catches one and rides it standing bolt upright with his arms at his sides, waiting for a bus on it.

“Orthodontist,” Skye says. “Fifty-four. Two ex-wives, both named Linda. He comes out at eight so he doesn’t have to say a word to anybody till his first patient, and his first patient is at ten, and he dreads her.”
“It’s Sunday.”
“It’s a very demanding practice.”
“He said hello to us.”
“He lifted his chin. That’s surfer for *please don’t*.”
“You don’t come out at eight on a Sunday in December to be alone,” Jack says. “You can be alone in bed.”

“You can be anything in bed,” Skye says, and puts a palm up at him. “Strike that. Watch. He’ll come in, and walk right past us, and get in his car and sit in it with the engine running and not go anywhere.”
They watch. He comes in on his belly on the last of the whitewater, and picks up his board, and walks up the beach toward the path, and stops beside the blanket with the water running off him.
“First time?” he says to Jack.
“Is it that obvious?”
“Keep at it. Took me till I was thirty to stand up like I meant it.” He goes on up the path. At the top a car door shuts, and they wait, and no engine starts.
“Sitting in it,” Skye says.
“He talked to us.”
“He talked to *you*.” She thinks it over with the cup at her mouth. “Split decision.”

They stay in the blanket till the sun gets down onto the cut bank. She tells him about Irene, who knitted socks for her grandchildren in a trailer between setups and never once got to fractions. He tells her about Sister Rose at St. Brigid’s, who wore a whistle on a lanyard and blew it at fifth-grade boys for breathing.
“Who wins?” she says. “Irene or the sister.”
“Sister Rose had a yardstick.”
“Irene had a union,” Skye says, and that settles it. At ten to ten she digs the white iPhone out of the towel and looks at it.
“Studio City by two. My mother does Sundays.” She puts it back. “Breakfast? The Starlite. Bev will say I look like somebody.”

“Your saints,” Skye says, and she’s already up, shaking the sand out of the blanket into the wind. “Go.”

She’s on her feet at the first syllable, knocking sand off the blanket. “Bev,” she says, folding it in half against the wind, “is going to *lose* it.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting.

body: Sully’s on a Saints morning is every television in the place talking at once, the brass bell over the corner table, and the first quarter half gone as Jack comes in out of the cold at twenty past ten. The table under the bell is Lena’s. She is up on the rung of her chair in black and gold with the cardigan knotted around her waist and the rope already off its cleat. Beside her Julian has a ginger ale and is learning a second religion, patiently. Joey Abruzzo is across from them in somebody’s Saints cap two sizes too small for him. Kevin has the end of the table, the napkin squared in front of him and the golf pencil beside it.
Laney has her forehead on the table and her enormous sunglasses on. “I’m observing a moment of silence,” she says, without lifting it. “It’s for me.”

At the end of the bar Dale Wisniewski is on his stool in the Barry Sanders jersey, and the owner has put the Lions on the set over the dartboard, in Baltimore, where it is going the way it usually goes.
Jack has salt dried white in his hair and sand still in the creases of his knuckles, and the cold of the water is somewhere under his sweatshirt yet. Lena doesn’t turn around from the screen.
“You smell like the ocean.”
Julian moves his chair over to make room, and Kevin moves the napkin.
Laney lifts her head off the table far enough to look at him over the sunglasses. She looks at his hair. “You’re *crusty*,” she says. Did you go in the *ocean*? It’s *December*.”
“Something like that.”
Laney looks at the salt, and then past him at Lena, who is watching the Falcons line up, and puts her head back down on the table.

It’s close all day, the kind of close that won’t let anybody at the table finish a plate of anything. Lena rings for every score and glares at the screen through everything else. Julian asks Kevin what a two-minute drill is, and means it, and Kevin draws him one on the corner of the napkin with arrows. Laney lifts her head for a field goal, says “Good for him,” and puts it back down. At the end of the bar the Lions get worse every time Jack checks on them, and Dale watches every snap of it anyway, and tips the bartender in quarters.

Early in the second quarter Julian leans over to Jack instead of Kevin. “Why does one man kneel and hold it for the other one? He could kick it off the ground.” “He could,” Jack says. “He’d miss.” He tells him about the holder: the snap coming back low and fast, the ball set down on its point in less than a second, the laces spun around to face the goalposts so the kicker’s foot never touches them, the kicker not looking at anything but the spot. Julian listens with his whole face, as he did with the tuning pegs. “So the kicker has to trust him completely.” “That’s the job.” From the rung of her chair Lena says to the television, not to either of them, “And when the holder fumbles it, it’s the kicker’s name in the paper,” and rings the bell once, for nothing, for emphasis.

At the half Lena takes a basket of fries down to the end of the bar and sits on the stool beside Dale’s for the whole of halftime, eating his fries with him and asking about Baltimore, and Dale tells her, at length, with his hands. Jack watches it from the table. Julian, beside him, is humming something under the halftime show, low, the same little phrase over and over. “Rudy’s mother,” he says, when he sees Jack hear it. “This morning. I’ve been trying to find the key she was in all day. I think it was her own.”
“I think it was.”
Julian nods, satisfied, and goes back to humming it.

In the fourth Hartley comes out to kick from thirty-eight with four forty-two left. Lena stops ringing and holds the rope in both fists, and the bar goes quiet for the holder, and it’s good. Then it’s the Falcons’ ball, and four minutes, and most of Sully’s can’t look. Lena can. She is standing on the rung with the rope wound twice around her hand and her knuckles white on it.
“Don’t you *dare*,” she tells the Saints. “Thirteen. Don’t you *dare*.”

journal.text: Dale Wisniewski. A Lions fan alone at the end of Sully’s bar in a Barry Sanders jersey. Warren, Michigan — not the other one. Tips in quarters. Said the rookie’s going to be good. Lions 38, Browns 37, on the last play. He bought me a root beer: the only man in California who knows what that cost. Thirteen and oh. Lena gave him the rope. For Detroit.

choices.text: Get up on the chair rung with her.
response: He gets up and steps onto the rung of the next chair, so his head is level with hers under the bell, a chair’s width off. She has the rope in both fists and doesn’t look at him, and the two of them stand up there over the table like lookouts on two masts while the Falcons come down the field.
And then there’s no clock left, and it’s thirteen and oh.

Lena rings it. She rings it until the glasses on the back bar answer, and Laney takes the sunglasses off to look at the ceiling, and Joey is standing on his chair, and Sully’s comes up all around her. s15b.slug: SUNDAY · 10:25 AM · THE STARLITE, UP THE 101
body: In daylight the Starlite is smaller. The star on its pole is sheet metal and cold tubing against a blue sky, five points and none of them lit, so from the on-ramp there’s no telling which two are dead. The sodium lamps are off over the diesel islands. The gravel is full of Sunday: a pickup with a Christmas tree roped down in the bed, a church van with its side door open, two rigs asleep nose to tail with their curtains drawn.

Bev is on. She’s behind the counter with the pencil through the clip in her hair and her reading glasses on a chain, and she watches them come in — a girl with wet hair in a sweatshirt with the neck cut out, a boy with salt in his eyebrows — and picks up the pot and follows them into the back.
Skye slides in on the window side of the booth. Jack takes the other. Bev pours, and doesn’t go. She studies Skye over the top of the glasses.
“Honey,” Bev says, “you look like somebody.”
“Everybody looks like somebody, Bev.”

body.text: “No,” Bev says. “I mean you look like you *slept*.”

body: Skye opens her mouth, and has nothing, and Bev takes the order out of it: a short stack and a side of bacon for the young lady, two over easy with hash browns and rye toast for the young man, and she goes back up front with the pot.
“She’s been waiting since Thanksgiving to do that,” Skye says. “She *workshopped* it.”

The pancakes come in a stack of three with a scoop of butter melting down the top. She butters between every layer anyway, and floods the plate with syrup from the sticky pitcher till it runs over the rim, and cuts the stack into a grid with the side of her fork, and eats. She eats with her elbows on the table. She talks with her mouth full. She points at him with the fork to make a point and drips syrup on his toast and calls it a tax.

The window beside her is full of the parking lot. A family is coming in from the church van, a little girl in a velvet dress and white tights skipping on the gravel. A trucker climbs down out of his cab in his socks. Skye has her eyes on her plate and on him, and she’s drawing a wave in the syrup with her fork to show him where he went wrong on the soft-top.
“You stand up too late,” she says. “You wait till you’re sure. The wave doesn’t wait for you to be sure. That’s the whole —” She shrugs with the fork. “Get up before you know.”
“That’s terrible advice.”
“It’s the only advice.” She eats a corner of the grid. “Ask anybody who’s ever stood up on anything.”
“That’s how people get married in Las Vegas.”
“That’s how people get *born*.” She points the fork. “Your Aquinas. Did he ever stand up on a board?”
“He was a very large man. They called him the Dumb Ox.” He takes the syrup away from her. “He’d have sunk it.”
“Then he doesn’t get a vote,” Skye says, and takes the syrup back.

She wants to know what Wednesday is. He tells her: Hale’s oral, twenty minutes each, and you defend somebody else’s best argument while Hale tries to take it away from you. “Whose?” “Somebody in the seminar.” “What’s the argument?” “A promise is made to a person. Not to a reason.” Skye puts the fork down, which she hasn’t done since the pancakes came. “Say it again.” He says it again. She turns it over with her eyes on the syrup. “So if the reason goes away, you still owe the person.” “That’s the argument.” “And if the person goes away?” He doesn’t have that one ready. “That’s Wednesday,” he says. “That’s a good Wednesday,” Skye says, and picks the fork back up. “I’d pay to watch that.”
At twenty to eleven his eyes go to the clock over the pass, an old one with a Coca-Cola girl on its face. She catches him at it.
“What are you missing?”
“A football game.”
“Go,” Skye says. “I’ll drive you.”
“No.”
She looks at him across the syrup and goes back to her pancakes.

She asks about the nineteenth instead. Who picks him up. “My dad. Pittsburgh. In the truck.” “The Lordstown man.” She does a line of his voice, low and flat, the Mahoning Valley in every vowel, and stops before it gets good. “Tell him the Saab says hello.” “He’ll say it’s GM.” “Tell him it’s an orphan now. Tell him it’s your fault.”
“What does she do on Sundays? Your mother.”

“Brunch. Notes on my week.” She mops a square through the syrup. “She’ll say I’m tan. She’ll say tan reads *summer*, and it’s December, and in January Cassidy goes off to a boarding school in Switzerland, and they have weather there.”
“Tell her you went to church.”
“I watched one from a car.” She looks at the square on her fork. “Yesterday. At five in the morning. Is that anything?”
“It’s a start.”
“Your Lady didn’t seem to mind,” Skye says, and eats it.
Bev brings the check face down and calls them *you kids*, and Skye pays it while he’s still digging for his wallet, and leaves a five on the Formica under her coffee cup for Bev, for the workshop.

She drops him at the Marine Lab turnout at half past eleven, at the chain, and he goes up to 412 and lies down on top of the covers in his sweatshirt with the salt still in his hair and is asleep in the time it takes to think about his boots.
At four minutes past one the RAZR buzzes on the desk, and two minutes later it buzzes again. He sleeps through both.
