body: At half past four the sun is twenty minutes off the water and comes through the blind in bars, and in the middle of 412, on her knees on the carpet in the gold of them, a tall girl with long black hair is filming Theo’s shoes. She works barefoot, in black, with the hair wound up out of the way and a pencil through it. The camera is a boxy chrome thing with BOLEX in script along its side. When she winds it by its little crank it makes the sound of a music box being wound, and when she lets it run it hums.

Theo made the introduction from the doorway when they came in, with the girl already looking at the room through the viewfinder. “Soledad is making a short about rich boys’ shoes. I’m the rich boy. Those are the shoes. Don’t look at the lens, Costigan. She hates that.” *Soledad.* The girl from the staircase at Halloween, with the clockwork camera, filming his straw hat from the landing while Theo told her *Don’t*.

So Jack is at his desk with his back mostly to it, and the legal pad from the Brick in front of him with Wednesday’s argument a few pages in, and the RAZR beside it, on and quiet. He has stopped pretending to write.

The shoes are on the carpet in a line from the door to the window, heel to toe: loafers in three colors, a pair of driving moccasins, boots that cost more than his father’s truck, a pair of brogues, the good cordovans, and at the end by the window a pair of white Keds with flowers painted on the toes in nail polish. Theo is on his bed in the navy robe with his ankles crossed, doing the voice-over.

“Ferragamo,” he says, as the lens comes down the line. “Rodeo Drive. A gift from my father’s second wife on my seventeenth birthday, a half size small, which I have chosen to believe was an accident.” The camera moves on. “Sperry. A boat in Cabo. My father’s idea of a conversation.” It moves on. “Visvim. Tokyo, by mail. They have never touched grass. Grass is for other people’s shoes.” At the brogues: “Church’s. I wore them to Mass once, as a joke. It didn’t take.”
The girl doesn’t answer any of it. Once the lens comes around to the desk and rests on the back of Jack’s neck, long enough that he feels it there, and goes back to the floor.
At the Keds Theo quits the voice-over. “Poppy,” he says. “Leave those in.” The girl stays on them, and he lets her.

When she gets to the window she stands up, still filming, and turns, and lets the lens go up the open closet: the hangers, the shirts that cost what shirts cost on Theo’s side of the room, the top shelf. The gray camera bag. The black duffel. She stops there.
“What’s in the black one?”
“Shoes,” says Theo.
The camera runs three seconds more on the shelf. She lowers it and lets the spring wind down.

She doesn’t pack anything. The Bolex goes on her hip by its strap, and she steps over the line of shoes without touching one, and on her way to the door she comes past Jack’s desk and looks down at him.
“Hi, hat,” she says.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad.

body: At nine on Gaudete Sunday the hull of St. Brendan’s holds candlelight up to the ribs, and the blue glass is black and full of the church’s own reflection. In the vestibule Joey Abruzzo has stopped Father Osei on his way to the procession to point at the vestments. They come out twice a year, and the other time is a long way off in Lent: old silk gone soft, rose, smelling faintly of the cupboard.
“It is not pink,” Osei says.
“Father, it’s a little —”
“It is *rose*, Joseph. Go and sit down.”

Lena and Julian have the pew in front, Lena in the mantilla with her missal, Julian with the hymnal already open and held low where she can read it. Jack takes the end of the next pew beside Kevin, where he usually is.

body.text: Kevin moves his coat over for him. “Thirteen and oh,” he says, low. “You’d have liked it.”

body: Gus brings the organ in, and the choir comes up the aisle behind the cross singing in Latin — *Gaudete, gaudete* — Gus’s own arrangement, all voices welcome and every one of them taking him up on it: Kenzie on top, Mrs. Fitch’s descant over Kenzie, Joey flat and proud at the back of the line. Beside Jack, Kevin sings the bass from the pew, steady and true, now that the whole Newman Center knows he can. At the wreath Kenzie peels off with a taper and lights the third candle, the rose one, beside the two violet, and the front pews sit back to look at it. In the pew in front Lena watches the new flame take, with her missal shut on one finger, until it stands up straight.

Zephaniah. The psalm, with Kenzie’s capo halfway up the neck. Paul to the Philippians: *Rejoice in the Lord always. I shall say it again: rejoice.* And then Luke, and John at the river, and the crowds coming down to him with a question.
Osei comes down out of the chair and stands at the head of the aisle in the rose vestments, with the bad leg resting.

“Three times in this Gospel people come to John with the same question,” he says. “The crowds. The tax collectors. The soldiers. *What then should we do?* And notice what John does not tell them. He does not say, leave your lives and come and eat locusts with me in the desert. He has eaten the locusts. He does not recommend them.” The church laughs, the low laugh of a full church at nine at night. “He says: you with two coats, give one away. You who collect the taxes, stop taking more than you are owed. You soldiers, be content with your pay. The next honest thing, in the life you already have.”

“And Zephaniah, who is not a cheerful man, says the strangest sentence in his book. *The Lord, your God, is in your midst. He will rejoice over you with gladness. He will sing joyfully because of you.*” He lets the church hold it. “God, singing. Over you. Over the soldier and the tax collector, and over the man who is still making up his mind about the coat.”

“Saint Paul says rejoice, and in case you were not listening, he says it again. Rejoice is a command, which means it isn’t a feeling. You can obey it on a bad week.” He looks out at the pews, at the backpacks under them and the finals in everybody’s faces. “Many of you are having a bad week. The candle is lit anyway.”
He goes back up to the chair, and the church sits in the quiet after it. Jack sits in it with his hands between his knees until the Creed stands him up.
At the sign of peace Lena turns around in the pew in front. “Peace.” And her hand. Julian turns with her and shakes Kevin’s hand, and then Jack’s, warmly, as he shakes everybody’s.

After Communion the choir gives them *Gaudete* again, softer, and on the last high note Mrs. Fitch’s descant cracks clean in half, and she finishes it anyway, louder, and Gus at the organ bows his head over the keys to keep his face to himself.

After the last hymn the church empties out toward the doors and the cold. Father Osei is on the top step in the rose vestments with the leg resting against the rail, shaking hands with everybody who comes past him. When it’s Jack’s turn he takes the hand in both of his.

body.text: “Mr. Costigan. Rejoice. It’s an order.”
body.else: “Mr. Costigan. The light is still on.”

body: Mrs. Fitch arrives at his elbow about candle wax on the carpet, and Osei lets go of Jack to hear about it.

journal.title: Fr. Gabriel Osei
journal.text: Newman chaplain. Kumasi, Ghana. Used to be a doctor. Limps and doesn’t mention it. Plays chess like he’s got all night and highlife like the neighbors owe him money. Told me a proverb about funerals. I laughed. That was apparently the point. Said Nonna’s Mass himself at the 12:10, like he promised. Gave me a card for her: ‘A grandmother likes paper.’ Blessed Hale’s deaf dog with his hand on its ribs, where it could hear. Finished Hale’s limerick for him. Laughed for a full minute at Becca’s crab. All Souls, at the book: ‘Write them all. He has a large book and a long memory.’ Saturday, behind the screen, one question: do I want to stop seeing her, or stop what happens. Change the hour. Keep her in the daylight. The Advent party: got the spray tan. Confiscated the mistletoe — he requested. At the sink he told me about the waiting room in Kumasi. His door is the one with the light on. Saturday I held the wrench for him at the courtyard wall. The sprinkler won. Gaudete: rejoice is a command.

s16a.slug: SUNDAY · 10:05 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE STEPS
body: Out on the steps the cold has come down hard and clear, and the stars are out over the Grove as far as the water. Behind them through the open doors the rose candle is still burning on the wreath, and Gus is playing the church empty.

People come out past them into the cold in twos and threes, pulling hats on, saying goodnight to the dark. Joey Abruzzo goes down the steps two at a time, telling Tyler about the vestments. Lena stops on the top step to button her coat, with the mantilla folded into her missal and the missal under her arm. “Gus let a Christmas carol into Advent.”
“It was in Latin.”
“That’s what Father Osei said.”
“Two coats,” Lena says, on the step, looking out at the cold. “Laney has fourteen. I’m going to tell her it’s binding.”

Julian goes down for the car. Kevin waits on the bottom step with his hands in the pockets of his quarter-zip. Lena takes the 8-Ball out of her coat pocket and shuts her eyes and asks it something, without moving her lips, and shakes it, and turns it up to the light over the doors to read it.
She laughs, surprised into it, and turns the little window around to show him.
*BETTER NOT TELL YOU NOW.*

body.text: “Your toy’s a coward, Jack.”
“Your saint’s a coward.”
“This thing’s a coward.”

response: “What did you ask it?”
Lena looks at him over the top of the ball, with the laugh still at the corners of her mouth. “Better not tell you now.” She puts it in her pocket.
“Ask it about Hale.”
She shakes it again and squints at the window. *Outlook good.* “It’s a liar,” Lena says. “I’m keeping it.”
He doesn’t say anything. She looks at the little window longer than it takes to read it, and turns it face down in her palm, and puts it away.

body: Julian’s headlights come along Ocean Road and stop at the curb below the steps, and he leans across inside and pushes the passenger door open. Lena goes down past Kevin with her hand in her coat pocket, and stops at the bottom, and looks back up.
“Goodnight, Jack.”
“Goodnight, Lena.”
Kevin says goodnight to Julian through the open door, and Julian says it back, and the door shuts, and the car pulls out toward Mission and goes. The RAZR in Jack’s pocket is on, and quiet.
Behind them the doors of St. Brendan’s swing to, and the blue glass goes on holding its candles over the Grove. Kevin zips the quarter-zip to his chin. “Wednesday,” he says. “Two o’clock. Hale.”
“Two o’clock.”
“You’ll be fine,” Kevin says. “You’ve been rehearsing since August.”
He walks back across Ocean Road with Kevin, toward the lit windows of Delgado and the last week of the semester.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. All Souls: she wrote her grandmother’s name in the book, and Nora Calloway’s. Nora was her host at Preview Weekend, in April. That night Wes ended it, on the phone, on the east stairs. He stopped going to Mass in September. There’s a ring. She knew something in September and decided not to notice — she says she’s good at it. At six in the morning she asked me what I’m going to do. She wrote Hale twelve pages in the spring of ’08, two years after the year she yelled at God. She’s had the same postcard the whole time. She knew mine on the porch. She had a house picked out on Zimple Street. A fig tree. She’d picked the paint. Veterans Day, on the bench above Campus Point: St. Martin gave the beggar half his cloak; she says everybody forgets the beggar took it. No. 9 for the reliquary. Friday the 13th, under the eucalyptus, in the middle of a sentence about monarchs: Julian asked her to dinner. So. Thursday night in the basement she played the piano properly — around the dead F. The last time she played it right in front of anybody was a November, four years ago. If you play well, she says, people ask you to play. Reading *New Moon* out of spite. Friday she signed the Manhattan Declaration from bed, with a cold. Two soups. She ate Julian’s. Mine’s on the sill for tomorrow. Ate Gloria’s soup cold out of the quart, at the sill, at six in the morning. Argued YES: a promise is made to a person, not to a reason. Wrote on my paper that I don’t believe one sentence of it. Neither does she. Mémère is lighting a candle for Nonna — the whole name. Half a name is half a candle. At the airport: Our Lady of Prompt Succor, for Nonna. She works fast. Thanksgiving: Theo said *pop* to the whole Broussard table. She asked about Theo, and Nonna, and her saint. Julian called during grace. Wes was in the kitchen. ‘Go back to your family, Youngstown.’ Handed Julian the bell rope at Sully’s. Knows I don’t work Mondays. Texted at two in the morning about Yusuf’s mother. On the lawn at four, looking at the place I wasn’t. Came to the Anchor at the end of my shift in Kevin’s car — Julian’s in Oakland, his brother’s home from the Navy. She has a paper. St. Nicholas Eve: Walgreens at half past one. I told her about Ma’s two hundred shoes; she said then we’re doing it, and we did every door in Delgado. Says I hold my phone like a hand of cards. Asked where I go. I said sometime. She said okay. Book Nine, for her Greek final: *Outis*. Nobody. In the laundry room she stepped back first. ‘Don’t make me be the one who wrecks something.’ Julian’s writing something she can’t hear yet. Twelve and oh in overtime. Her free hand found Kevin. Knows Book Nine by heart; asked me to pray at eight. Picked my best argument at the Brick: what a man says yes to. Put her phone face up next to mine and said nothing. Heard Julian’s song before anybody. ‘It’s good, Jack. It’s really good.’ Told me not to leave in the second chorus. The Advent party: I kept the whole room between us all night. She brought coffee to the white elephant, and I got it. Stole my 8-Ball. Won an argument about ‘Joy to the World’ with Isaac Watts. Didn’t play. Julian did. Friday night, half past twelve, she knocked on 412; Theo said the library. At the Mañanitas she told me about Juan Diego, who took the long way around the hill. Thirteen and oh — she gave the rope to Dale. After the Gaudete Mass she asked the 8-Ball something. Better not tell you now.
